Right Hon. AY. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
That on and after Monday, the 19th of April instant, and on and after Wednesday, the 21st April instant, and all subsequent Mondays and Wednesdays until the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence after questions and notices of motions for production of papers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT MEASURES ON MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
believe the government really and seriously want both days all at once. I am speaking on behalf of my hon. friends to my left who, I see, have a great many notices of motions on the order paper.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT MEASURES ON MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY
speechtext:
I
would suggest that the leader of the opposition just speak for his own party.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT MEASURES ON MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY
speechtext:
I would have confined myself to doing so, but I see evidences of the arrangement in the silence of hon. gentlemen to my left. I do not like to assume that they put these motions on the order paper merely for display, but that seems to be the conclusion from the remarks of the leader of the Progressive party. However, we did not put our motions on the order paper for that purpose. I know, of course, that it will be necessary to take an increasing share of the days of private members, but unless the rules are amended, or at least the time deferred, it
Rural Credits

really becomes absurd to place important motions on the order paper at all. It is true that some motions have been called, but that does not affect the case, because if those motions had been moved the others could not have been. All the motions that could have been moved have been moved within the time allotted. Personally, I would not object to Wednesday being taken; I think it is usual to take Wednesday first and withhold Monday for a little time. We will get through as fast as possible; but there are fouf or five pretty important resolutions for the discussion of which an opportunity should be afforded. I would ask the government to amend the motion so as to limit it to Wednesday-I have no objection to that- leaving Monday still available for the business of private members of the House.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT MEASURES ON MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY
speechtext: I should like to endorse what has been said by the leader of the opposition. It seems to me there are several motions on the order paper that are of importance. subtopic: PRECEDENCE FOR GOVERNMENT MEASURES ON MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY

jection just for the present, %vithout committing the government for any period of time, to eliminate that part of the resolution which relates to Mondays and have it relate only to Wednesdays. Then we will strike out the words "on and after Monday the 19th, instant", and the motion will read:
On and after Wednesday the 21st, instant, and cn all subsequent Wednesdays to the end of the session, government notices of motion and so forth shall have precedence.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, April 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 17 to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919-Hon Mr. Stewart-Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Revaluation of land sold to settlers.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For the convenience of hon.
members the proposed amendments, as nearly as I could gauge the desire of the committee, have been drafted and hon. members will find them on their desks. The number of the bill is the same but hon. members will use the reprint in which the amendments appear.
In our discussion the other afternoon a very wide field was covered and with the Soldier Settlement Board I have gone carefully over the suggestions that were made in the committee, but I find there are innumerable difficulties in meeting all the requests. One of the most persistent and apparently one that was voiced by almost every member was that the soldier who might be desirous of re-establishing himself on his own land after revaluation should be given consideration. Owing to the provisions of the old act we find it exceedingly difficult to do that without a

great deal of amendment, and after discussing the matter thoroughly with the board we came to the conclusion that in cases where there was a desire on the part of the soldier to re-establish himself on his own land, we would have to hold up the final closing out of his agreement, because after all it is nothing more nor less than an agreement with the board to purchase, and give him an opportunity, if he was able to re-establish himself, to come back on his land.
I am well aware that a much wider field was discussed, and I pointed out to the committee that owing to the fact that a very large number of these farms had already been disposed of and more of them were allocated, the large bulk of the land, if you can call it that, that would be left, would be land of very inferior quality and land upon which, of course, there would be a pretty heavy depreciation before it was sold. After discussing the matter thoroughly, I came to the conclusion that the best thing we could do in that case was to follow the suggestion of the board and notify immediately the party who was being closed out that he would be given a reasonable period of time in which to re-establish himself on his own land. Beyond that I do not think we can go. I discussed the matter with some of the members of the House pointing out our difficulties and they appeared to agree with me in that particular, that beyond that we could not very well go.
If the land is completely closed out, the provisions of the old act rather debar the soldier from securing the land, but we will use our best endeavours to place any man back on his land if the land is available and to give him an opportunity of taking advantage of the revaluation for which the soldiers themselves have been contending. That was the conclusion we came to in order to meet that objection.
The other contention was as to the method of revaluation and hon. members will see in the reprint of the bill our definition, as regards those who would be dealt with, of how depreciation will be computed. That is in paragraph (c) of section 68. It reads:
The difference or depreciation in value to be determined shall be the diminution, not due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, in the present market value of the land as compared with the price at which the soldier agreed to purchase the said land from the board; provided that in any case where the actual sale price is greater than the maximum amount which under section 16 of this act may be advanced by the board in the purchase of land on behalf of any settler, such maximum amount shall be deemed the sale price for the purposes of this section.

Soldier Settlement Act
That is the provision we made as to the method to be followed by the committee in arriving at a decision as to how much the depreciation, if any, should be on any given soldier settler's land.
In paragraph (e) we have provided for the composition of the district arbitration committee. I found a very wide variation of opinion amongst members of the committee with respect to how this should be done. Some were strongly in favour of having the whole matter left to the decision of the county court or district court judge. Others favoured an arrangement to be arrived at if possible between representatives of the Soldier Settlement Board and the soldiers themselves with provision for appeal in case of dispute. Having in mind the desirability of shortening this and trying to meet the view's of the committee as far as possible, I decided to embody in the provisions of this paragraph the views of the board, that is to make the judge chairman of the board v'ith a representative from the Soldier Settlement Board to be named by that board and a representative of the soldiers themselves. This would not involve any serious departure from the request that they be dealt with by the board where at all possible, but it would provide that the judge would sit on every case. The judge would be chairman of the committee and there would be one hearing which would be final. That would obviate the necessity of an appeal and it would bring the hearing close to the soldier's home, because as hon. members will notice, later on there is a provision that the hearing * be held within the district of the county court or district court judge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does that apply to every
case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, there
is no appeal.
The majority of the board would govern.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it would have to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is to say the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, the soldier and the judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. They would have equal authority with the judge, although undoubtedly in every case the judge as chairman of the board would exercise considerable influence. It would be useless to deny that if the two representatives were in agreement the judge would simply ratify that agreement; but where they disagree he will
be in exactly the same position as in the case of an appeal. The rest of the amendment is intended to conform with the previous changes as provided for in the act. These are the principal changes that are effected by the amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I shall speak only for a few minutes and on one point, namely, the settlement of the question of revaluation. I do not think that the minister apprehends the entire effect of the plan he has suggested. If I understand it, that plan is that in the case of every revaluation there shall be a board composed of a judge of the county court, a representative named by the Soldier Settlement Board and, I presume, the veteran himself or someone acting in his behalf. Who selects the third man? Is it the soldier himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, if there is no veterans' organization in the locality.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And if there is one the organization selects the third man. I do not know what the minister expects to gain by that. I am so satisfied that it is not in his own interest to go on with that proposal that I am rather surprised at his having brought it in. In the first place it leaves the situation precisely as it was before in regard to all those cases in which the board and the settler are agreed on the valuation. In that event the situation is just the same as if there never was a board at all, for all they have to do is to go before the judge, who sits there powerless. Why go through the mummery of having a court if that is to be the proceeding? Of course I want the court, but such a court as this is a mere mockery. In every case where the representative of the board and the representative of the soldier himself are at one the judge has no more to say about it than if he were a wooden god. Consequently the minister's representatives will simply be given carte blanche to the treasury of the country in respect of all that wide sweep of cases, in fact over the whole thing, inasmuch as they can agree on any price they like. So that the minister would be in a position, if the representatives were such as have represented governments before, to do what he liked with the treasury to the extent of the whole value of the lands to be revalued. It is not right. The principle itself is wrong; it is false.
Suppose the minister leaves the other two representatives out: see where he is. He is in a splendid position in every single case, because the county court judge then fixes the valuation. The representative of the board
Soldier Settlement Act

and the soldier's representative are both there, and they can argue the facts and produce witnesses; but the judge fixes the valuation and that settles it, so that the minister has no responsibility. Furthermore, the machinery is infinitely more simple, and is less expensive.
I cannot see the slightest thing in the world to be gained by putting these two men on with the judge. I do not think I idolize judges more than I should, but I'submit that it is unfair to a judge to put a veteran's representative or a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board on a parity with himself. I do not think it is treating the bench as it ought to be treated by this House. I do not suggest that judges would refuse to act; I do not suppose they would. Indeed, I think that every one would help in any way he could. But we have to preserve the dignity of the bench, not for the sake of the bench, but for the sake of the people and in the interests of the administration of justice. This is not doing so. I therefore criticize the proposal on two grounds principally; first, that it leaves the minister carte blanche, just as was the case before; and secondly, that it is much more expensive than the other method I suggest and that no purpose can be served by it. And I add a third ground, namely, that it is not fair to the judiciary to put untrained men on a parity with a judge in the hearing of evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Why more
expensive?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Because you will have
to pay the representatives. If you create a board with a veterans' representative on it. you will have to pay him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We may
have to pay one representative, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly, and to that
extent it will be more expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We should
have to pay him in any case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, I do not think so.
If a soldier comes before the board for revaluation I do not see why it should be essential to pay a lawyer to act for him, although I have no objection to that course if the minister so desires."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would not be a lawj'er.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Or anyone else who
might represent the soldier. It may be wise to pay someone to represent him, but that is so much more added to the cost. The minister's plan is vulnerable at every point and

I cannot see what he hopes to gain by it. In the honest administration of his office, in the faithful performance of this task, which I assume to be his only motive, he has nothing in the world to gain by having these two representatives acting in conjunction with the judge. On the other hand he has everything to gain by placing the whole responsibility on the judge, who in the fulfilment of his oath of office can assess the value of the land. To make the judge share that responsibility with others, indeed, to shift the whole responsibility from him whenever the soldier and the representative of the board agree, is to make a mockery of the bench and of the law as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There seems to be considerable aversion to the cold application of the law in cases of this kind. I confess there is a good deal in the argument of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), but I have received representations from various sources confirming the advisability, with a view to settling the matter as expeditiously as possible, of having an arrangement made between the representatives of the board and the soldier himself, and in the event of such an agreement not being reached, of referring the matter to a judge. When the. two were in agreement I cannot conceive that the judge would have very much to say on the question. He might review the case; he might criticize the agreement; and he might consider in certain cases even where there was an agreement that he had a right to interfere. And undoubtedly the weight of his counsel would have considerable effect upon both parties. It is not uncommon for a judge to act in such a capacity; judges have been doing so on commissions of various kinds where they did not exercise absolute control. I thought therefore that in this way the matter might be expedited. I do not like the idea of appeals, and it was in order to meet the point of view suggested by the various proposals submitted to me by the committee that I embodied this plan in the bill. I cannot agree with my hon. friend that it will cost more to have the county judge deal with it absolutely as a judge after listening to the representations made by each side. I am well aware, of course, of the method pursued in many cases of disputed assessment,-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And in expropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; but I
do not fear what he anticipates, that the judge's hands will be tied. Indeed I think he will exercise all his discretionary powers in each case. Where there is disagreement the

Soldier Settlement Act
judge will agree with either one or other of the contestants, and that is what he usually does in every case that comes before him. This commends itself to me as the best method of speedily settling the whole matter. The Soldier Settlement Act is not changed in any particular with respect to the board. The board has pretty wide powers under the act. With those powers I have never attempted to interfere, and I do not propose to do so now. On the other hand, I cannot say that I have ever had very strong representations from soldier settlers as to what should be the composition of the board to deal with their cases. A great many of them say they are perfectly willing to leave the adjustment to a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board. Of course, one might infer that the board would be too generous, but I rather gathered the trend of the discussion in the House was that generally the board was not generous enough in dealing with the soldiers. My thought is that this will commend itself to the committee as a fair and equitable method of reaching an adjustment.

:	I should like to add a word
or two to what my leader has said in connection with the method proposed by the minister. I cannot see any object whatever in having a committee of three. As has been said, if the two representatives agree the judge becomes a figure-head, the case is pre-judged and the decision is really reached before the case gets to him at all. On the other hand, if there is any disagreement-and I would be inclined to think if each did his duty there would be disagreement-it practically means the decision of the judge alone. Surely the minister must realize it will cost a great deal more, if there are going to be thousands of applications, for instead of the county judge presiding you will have a committee of three members. Surely to goodness the judge alone can hear the evidence quickly and reach a decision which will be fair to the soldiers. I am given to understand that members of the House who have been interesting themselves in this matter have received letters from many soldier settlers indicating a desire on their part that the county judge alone should dispose of these cases. I commend the minister for one change he has made; that is, each case must go before the county judge. I think it would have been unfortunate if the clause had stood as it was originally introduced. Now there cannot be much delay, nor can there be much expense. I am not going to advocate that the department should pay a lawyer to appear for the soldier settler. I think myself he can get people in the vicinity to give evidence as 14011-151

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: to the value of the land. I certainly agree with the minister that there should be no appeal. None has been suggested, as I understand, and none is provided. So we are in accord with that. Certainly it will save the country thousands of dollars to leave the matter to the county judge, and for the reasons I have stated it seems to me you will get a satisfactory decision in that way. If the case goes to the committee without being prejudged, it will be his decision which in the end will govern. You will have one arbitrator seeking a high valuation on behalf of the soldier, and presumably you will have someone on behalf of the department seeking a low valuation. The judge may make one come down a little and the other go up a little, but after all it is what he thinks is proper and he gives the decision.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the question of delay, my hon. friend is not arguing that because the committee are sitting rather than the judge it would occasion delay?
I am not going to say it would increase the delay a great deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Nor the
cost.

It goes without saying that if you have three people to agree on the date for the hearing it is going to take longer to get them in accord. The practice in Ontario which obtains in connection with overholding tenants would, to my mind, be the practice to adopt in cases of this kind. Application is received, and immediately the parties go before the judge and ask him for an appointment, which is soon arranged, and the judge at the time appointed hears the case and decides it. So while I am not arguing that the delay would be very much greater, it would certainly be greater to some extent. My main point is that you have a more satisfactory tribunal when you have the county judge, and the country might as well be saved the extra expense that a committee of three would entail.
A very excellent practice has been adopted by the various ministers in showing in italics all amendments to their bills. That practice has not been followed with this bill, perhaps through lack of time, but as a member of the House I do hope that excellent practice will be followed in future. It is so much easier to follow any proposed changes in a bill when they are printed in italics.
Mr. Chairman, I am in a position to give the committee some direct information of the opinion of the soldier settlers in regard to this matter. The right

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: hon. leader of the opposition, not so much to-day but the other day when we were on the bill, emphasized the point that in his opinion there was danger of the soldier settler's representative and the political appointee, the second man, getting together in more or less collusion in order to cut the price down to the applicant soldier to make themselves good fellows with the soldier and thereby secure political influence. That is not the view entertained, at least by one fairly large body of soldiers in the district I represent. They have been hard hit by the old act and are hoping for a considerable reduction in the valuation of their farms. They are fairly well organized. I had a wire from them a few days ago, I have not it with me, but the gist of it is this. The bill contemplated a board to be composed of one man, the appointee of the government, being a Soldier Settlement Board man, one by the soldiers and a third by the government also. They object to that on grounds the very opposite to those expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition. They seemed to fear that the government having two members on the board might be unfair to them, not too lenient. From past experience there is always a certain amount of antagonism between the man collecting debts and enforcing regulations and the party with whom he is dealing. While their whole point of view was not set out at length in the wire, it was to the effect that they did not think it was fair to them to have two men on the board appointed by the government. They wanted to have the third man appointed by the first two. I wired back that two alternatives had been suggested: one, that the third man should be the county court judge; the other -the proposal of the right hon. leader of the opposition-that the county court judge should be the sole arbiter. I asked them which of the two in their judgment they would prefer. They wired back at once to say they would be satisfied if the third man were a county court judge. I merely give that opinion for what it is worth, but there is a considerable body of men; they know what they want; they know local conditions and that is their point of view.

Mr. Chairman, I would strongly urge upon the minister that he leave this matter to a county court judge alone. If the soldier wants to have his land revalued he must find a representative to sit on this board. In the district which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) represents 
there is a body of soldiers probably one hundred in number. Is that not correct?
No, that is not correct. Call it 250.

There is a large number, at any rate. The fact is that in British Columbia farm lands generally have depreciated in value by almost 50 per cent since 1920, according to the statistics of the Department of Agriculture. That condition obtains all over British Columbia, and I imagine that in the district represented by my hon. friend the depreciation is greater than that; it is 50 per cent, at least. That will mean a great many arbitrations, and the soldiers will have to find representatives for each of these arbitrations. That means expense, because no man is going to sit as the third arbitrator for a period of months without some recompense. Who is to pay him-the soldier? He cannot pay because he has not the money; many of them have not enough money to buy clothing; they have been sticking it out for years waiting for a chance to get on their feet. They have had a heavy load to carry, a heavy indebtedness to meet yearly and they have not the money to pay an arbitrator. Then who is going to initiate these proceedings? The soldier must take the responsibility of initiating the proceedings, but who is to do it for him? Solicitors are not plentiful in the district which my hon. friend represents.

There are enough solicitors
for our needs.

A few miles away, in all
probability. There may be enough solicitors, but I know the solicitors on Vancouver island fairly well, and they are not very plentiful. They all have to earn a living. Who is going to pay the solicitors to initiate and continue the proceedings for the men who want to have their lands revalued? Who is to pay the solicitors, or the solicitor retained on behalf of a group of men? The proceedings will be costly enough without having a board of three men on every arbitration. Every arbitration conducted by such a board is going to take longer than would a county court judge sitting alone, because all the members of that board will have questions to ask; they are not men experienced in arbitrations, and the proceedings will be prolonged unnecessarily. On the other hand the county court judge knows how such proceedings should be carried on, and he is qualified to give decisions in judicial

Soldier Settlement Act
matters such as these. I suggest that this wording is very vague indeed, as to how this representative is to be chosen.
A representative of the veterans' organization in the district.
Supposing there is no soldiers' organization in a particular district? I know that on certain islands on the British Columbia coast there is perhaps only one soldier
4 p.m. settler; who is going to act for him? Who is he to appoint to represent him on the board? Can he act himself, may I ask the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he can.
Then we have this delightful anomaly of a man acting for himself-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But what is the judge going to do to shorten these proceedings? My hon. friend is raising a barricade of difficulties now and I would like to ask him again wherein the judge will shorten the time expended?

I am coming to that. Of
course there are going to be difficulties; I am pointing out difficulties which I expect the minister to meet and which it is his duty to meet. These points have been brought out before, and I am surprised that the minister has not come back with a solution for them. Either we have this strange anomaly, if the soldier can act as his own representative on that board-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
say that he could act as a member of the board; I said that he might appear and give evidence.

I must have misunderstood
the minister, but I certainly understood him to say distinctly that the soldier himself could act as a member of this board of arbitration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
say anything of the kind.
Then supposing there is no soldiers' organization in a particular district, I would like to ask who is going to represent the soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at the provisions of the act he will see that the soldiers, either by themselves of by their organizations, may nominate someone for that purpose, but not the individual soldier whose case is being tried.

The words I am looking
at are:
-and one a representative of the veterans' organization in t'he district.
14011-151J
Supposing there is no such organization in that district?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will surely admit that where there are three or four settlers, they may organize themselves. That section which my hon. friend read is to give the men absolute scope in choosing the third member of the board.

I am pointing out to the
minister the case where there may be no settlement. I know of one instance where a soldier settler is on an island about 135 miles north of Vancouver; that man is the only settler on the island.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is he in a
judicial district?
Possibly so, but think of all the trouble that man will have in finding a soldiers' organization 100 miles away, and then saying to someone, "You come over here and act as my representative."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the
soldier is furnished with a form upon which to make his application, with all the information necessary for the consideration of his claim embodied in that form, surely he can fill it in without the aid of a solicitor.

He will certainly need: a
solicitor or someone to take his affidavit, which is provided for in the early part of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He can go before any justice of the peace, and if that man is 150 miles away his case will get the same consideration; it will be examined by the board and will be presented to the tribunal by the board. I have asked my hon. friend before wherein the difference would lie between going 'before this tribunal and appearing before a county court judge?

I will answer that question
now. In the first place the proceedings before a county court judge will be much more expeditious than those before three men inexperienced in judicial proceedings. Secondly, the proceedings before a judge will be very much -more economical to the man than the proceedings before such a tribunal. Because, I maintain, somebody must pay this soldier's representative. You must either have a man chosen at random for each particular arbitration, a man who knows nothing about arbitration proceedings, to act on behalf of the individual soldier, or you must have one man-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend is again building up a barricade.
Soldier Settlement Act

You would not have more than one member of the arbitration board in any judicial district. My hon. friend is not suggesting that every individual case has a different arbitrator?

That is my point. Let me
put myself in the position of the soldier settler. I have been struggling there for three or four years. My neighbour may be quite satisfied with the particular representative for his man on the board. I might say "No; that man will not do for me, I will not have him at any cost. If I am to be entitled to somebody to look after my interests on that board then I insist upon having some voice in the choice of that man. He must be my nominee." I would not submit, and I am certain the soldiers in any district would not submit to what is proposed here.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
May I ask
my hon. friend another question:	In the adjustment of pensions under the soldiers' civil re-establishment is there not a paid individual who acts on behalf of the soldiers in every province? My hon. friend is aware of that?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, did my hon. friend ever hear any individual soldier say that this man was not going to be permitted to act for him?

That is quite a different
matter. That man is not adjudicating on his case, he is an advocate.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That does not prevent the soldier from having any representation made before the board on his behalf through anybody he likes.

I am afraid the minister
does not appreciate the case at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely my
hon. friend would not suggest that we should have anything so cumbersome as changing the arbitrator for every individual case. The one committee would deal with every case in the judicial district.

Then if that is the minister's intention I say emphatically that the individual soldier has no representation on that board at all, none whatever, and it would be far better to trust himself in the hands of a judge, who is sworn to do his duty and who is trained in judicial matters, than to trust himself in the hands of somebody appointed in the manner proposed to look after his interests on the board. I may be a soldier

and I may be quite satisfied to have the minister, for instance, as my representative on that board.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg my
hon. friend's pardon.

I say that I as a soldier
settler may be quite satisfied to have the minister act for' me on the board, if that were possible, or I may prefer somebody else. If the soldier on the land is to be represented on this board of arbitrators then he must have some voice in the selection of that third man. On the other hand the minister's suggestion is that the same man shall represent the soldiers on the board in a particular district. He asks me wherein it would be easier if the judge alone were acting and I tell him this: If the same board acts in fifty or two hundred and fifty cases you must pay that board. Who is going to pay the costs? Is the soldier going to pay the costs of his representative on the board? Is that man to be paid remuneration from day to day for each day that he sits?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The representative of the soldier?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, undoubtedly. You could not expect the soldiers to pay this man themselves. The government will have to pay him.
Under what authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is provided for in the bill.

I read there:
Expenditures necessarily incurred by any district arbitration committee shall be paid out of monies appropriated from time to time by parliament to soldier land settlement.
That means the expenditures incurred. That does not mean they are entitled to any special remuneration. That does not entitle the Land Settlement Board, or the government, to pay the soldiers' representative one penny as far as I can see. Personally I would feel inclined to move an amendment unless the minister can see his way clear to reconsider this provision. I think such a board is an absurdity, I think it will be cumbersome, I think it will be unfair to the soldier, and that the minister will be well advised to leave this matter with the county judge. I think the same people will be brought into operation if the county court judge is acting alone as will be brought in here. In this way: The board will get together and they may agree upon a fair valuation based upon independent

Soldier Settlement Act
reports. In that case an application can be made before the judge to confirm a certain valuation without any long-winded hearing of evidence, but upon proper affidavits or proper valuations from independent sources. The judge determines at this sitting in a judicial capacity. The responsibility is his to peruse these valuations and affidavits. If these two men cannot go and make this application before the judge by consent it must mean a more or less contested application in each case, the judge and the two arbitrators hearing the evidence viva voce, and giving a decision upon that evidence. That will mean that valuators, and so on, will have to go before the board personally and give their evidence as to valuation, whereas if the county court judge is sitting alone the soldier may get independent valuators to go before him in case of a contest, and the independent evidence will convince the judge very easily. Or the two representatives together will go before the judge with affidavits by agreement after having arrived at a valuation which they consider fair. I feel very strongly that this section should be amended and the judge alone made the sole arbitrator from the points of view of expense and of fairness to the soldier concerned.

I just want to make sure of
paragraph (g). I think we can apprehend its meaning but I will read it:
Expenditures necessarily incurred by any district arbitration committee shall be paid out of monies appropriated from time to time by parliament to soldier land settlement.
I understand the purpose of that paragraph is to devise a means to pay these two representatives. Am I right or wrong in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
quite catch my hon. friend's question.

I am dealing with paragraph
(g) which I have just read, and I take it for granted the purpose of that paragraph is to provide funds to pay the members of this committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There will
be the necessary expenses, yes.

That would be their travelling expenses, of course, and there would be a per diem allowance. I think we may assume the per diem allowance would not be less than $10 a day, at least. With two men to provide for that would be 120 apart, from the county judge. Now, I do not know whether the minister has reached a decision as to what the policy of the department is to be in connection with this valuation. Suppose, for instance, the soldier makes application for a
revaluation and he claims that the land should be worth only four thousand whereas he paid six thousand. Suppose the department is of the opinion that the valuation of four thousand which he sets is altogether too low. Would it be the intention of the department to provide counsel, on its behalf to appear and to contest his application with some degree of vigour as would be done in any ordinary case before the Exchequer court, or is it the intention of the department merely to leave the soldier on the one hand, and perhaps to have some lay representative of the department, prepare the case and go before the county judge? I would be almost inclined to think that the department, when they were contesting a case, would want to follow it up with some degree of vigor, and would probably have some qualified person present to act for them. What about the soldier? I know a few in my own county, but we have not very many there. From what I have heard in regard to this matter, there must be many soldiers who could not afford the expense of securing counsel to appear for them and present their case, and there is no provision in the bill regarding costs. Suppose a soldier without means, but with a good case, having confidence in it, decides to go before the board and wins his case; is he to be at the entire expense of securing counsel if that be necessary? Is he to find money for witnesses? Is this board to be in a position to award to that soldier, in case of success, a reasonable allowance for expenses? I think if he succeeds he should get his expenses. Of course if a soldier presents a case which has no merit and fails, he should not get costs. In such an extreme case, if the soldier were worth anything, perhaps he should be made to pay some of the costs. I am not advocating that proposition, but that could be argued and I want to present that feature of the case to the minister.
I want to make a concrete suggestion in the first instance. The fee for counsel would be $10 a day or more, and might easily be $20, but I am satisfied it would not be less than S10 for each of the men. I should think, if you had much of a contest, the average dura-, tion of a case would be a day, two days or perhaps a day and a half, which would mean two days. There you have two days at $10, and that would mean an expense of $40. I would suggest that you should make an allowance to the soldier of anything he saves in revaluation. If he demonstrates he has a good case, he should be allowed $30 or $40 at least, which would be merely the cost this legislation is going to impose upon the country, and give that to the soldier to get
Soldier Settlement Act

an expert witness as to valuation. If you want to go a step further, I would be prepared to support the proposition that where a soldier brings his claim before a judge and succeeds he should be allowed reasonable expenses in pressing his claim. It is done in the Exchequer court and every other court
I have not heard a word from the minister as to what good he thinks is going to be accomplished by a membership of three on this committee. What suggestion does he make? If there is disagreement between the two the judge will decide anyway, therefore why not let the judge deal with the matter? It will certainly be less expensive. The case will not last as long, and if you want to dispose of a little of the country's money, instead of giving it to useless men on the board-not useless as far as the men are concerned, because the judge will ultimately decide the case-use that money to help that soldier press his claim. I would make it contingent upon his success, because if he chooses to bring a case asking for a re-valuation in the hope of getting a lower value placed on the land, and fails, I should not suggest that he should get any of the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Nor any
assistance to bring the case?

I did not say the soldier
should get any assistance if his case is not meritorious. I can quite understand that if you put in a provision allowing a certain sum in cash to the men, it would be an incentive, perhaps, to bring eases that were none too meritorious. I do not go that far at all, but where there is merit, I say we should help the soldier, and I certainly think there must be very many meritorious cases. In my own county the returned soldiers may be better off and may have greater opportunities than in some of the remote parts of the country, but I feel satisfied there is not one that really has the money to properly handle his case before the judge, and in the west, of course, the costs are heavier. What are the witness fees to be paid? Suppose you confine yourself to the law obtaining in my province and probably in other provinces. The law permits the calling of three experts. Where are you going to get three experts out west to travel a hundred miles to attend a hearing, unless you have a nice little sum at your disposal? Where is the money to come from Is the soldier not to be put in a position to secure redress? You have a provision in the bill that, where the applicant is successful, out of any award that is made a sum is paid in cash, I believe it

is going to be the policy of the department to employ counsel. I am not saying it in a nasty spirit but it is done in all cases. If the department has counsel, in what position is the soldier placed, if he has not money and cannot get competent witnesses, to say nothing about employing an advocate of sufficient ability and experience to properly plead his case
Dealing with the question of arbitrators, you have two tribunals, one is the ordinary judicial tribunal where you have a judge presiding. The other is a board of arbitrators. As far as I know in all arbitrations you have one arbitrator selected by one of the parties concerned and the other arbitrator selected by the other party. It is the duty of those two arbitrators to do their utmost to secure the best results for those who appoint them. Then the third arbitrator is, as a rule, selected by those two arbitrators and is supposed to be an independent man. In this case the soldier is not going to have the same right in that regard. The department will have a man there who will be specially instructed, whose duty it will be to keep that man as near to the original value as possible, because. I take it for granted the department would not fight a case if they did not think they had a right to do it. They would be willing to agree to a lower valuation before going to court if they had doubt about the matter. They are going to fight to keep the valuation up. Who will appear before the tribunal with the same degree of interest on behalf of the soldier? I do not say that there would not be any representative of the soldier. I have a great deal of faith in the representatives of the soldiers on our various boards, and I have nothing to say against them. I think it would be the desire on the part of the veterans' organization and the Soldier Settlement Board to do whatever they could for the soldiers, but nobody suggests that that representative would have the same interest as the soldier himself, or as the representative of a party to an arbitration would have.
For the reasons I have given, I think the minister should leave this with the county judge in the district, and if he wants to hand out any money, instead of giving it to the members of that committee, who are not going to improve the situation but will of course impose expense on the country, better take that $30 or $40 and give it to the soldier to help him present his case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I agree
with a great deal of what the hon. member has said, particularly with his remarks in respect to arbitration. I do not share in his

Soldier Settlement Act
fear about the soldier not being represented, but I do share his view that the representative of the soldier and the Soldier Settlement Board are very likely-
I did not say the soldier would not be represented. I said he would not be as well represented on that committee by the appointee named by the government as he would by an appointee named by himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member is wrong in speaking of an appointee named by the government. Bear in mind that the representative who will be on the committee will be a member of the Soldier Settlement Board; he will be named by them.
It does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes he is
to be named by the Soldier Settlement Board.

The sub-section provides that
the minister may appoint a district arbitration committee, and one of them shall be the county judge and two others are named, one from the Soldier Settlement Board and one from the veterans organization in the district.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Surely the machinery is there to make the appointment. I was seeking to get away from this thing entirely as minister. Of course, I cannot get away from the responsibility of it any more than the minister can get away from the responsibility of the Soldier Settlement Act, but surely the House does not hold the minister responsible for all the doings of the Soldier Settlement Board. He is, as minister, responsible for the board, but the board itself will name the representative who will sit on this arbitration committee.
The bill does not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It says
through the minister. The minister is in charge of the board. If necessary I will change it to the effect that the board will do the appointing, if that will help the matter in any way, but I do not think it will.

If the minister is going to make any changes, he should change the composition of the committee. Will he give us some good reason why he wants three members on the committee instead of just the county court judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I pointed
out a moment ago that where one of the representatives on the committee is a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, he is a government official and as it is the actions
of the board that are on trial, he will be liable to protect the interests of the government. That, I think, is a fair argument. On the other hand I leave it to the local soldier organization to appoint their representative.

That is just where the
minister falls down. Under the correct wording of that section the minister himself as head of the department designates a man who comes from a particular class, a representative of the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But to be
named by the organization.

That is not what the bill
says.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend want the organization to name the man and that he shall be appointed?

If the minister must have it,
but that is not what I want at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am
willing to do that. I am willing to step as far away from this thing as possible for political advantage or otherwise, but I want the committee to understand what we are trying to do and I want to argue why I think the arbitration committee is preferable to the judge alone. I am going to base myself on the very argument presented by my hon. friend, and that is this. I do not want the representative of the soldier to be changed on every individual case; neither will any of my hon. friends contend that. The judge has jurisdiction within the particular district, and if he is to be the sole arbitrator he will deal with every individual case in that whole judicial district. I fail to see why anyone should desire that every little corner should have a special representative. Surely they can agree upon some man who will present their case. I admit at once and I do not think anyone will deny that the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board will be named for the judicial district and will sit on every case in that district.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
By the
Soldier Settlement Board, or by the government, if you will. There is no objection to that, I take it. Then you are right in the face of my hon. friend's argument that this result will come about, namely, that you have the client represented, of course, by a representative of himself on the board and naturally the representative will bring him with him because he will appear there-
Soldier Settlement Act

I object to that statement,
"of course." That person is not appointed by him. It is true that a person is appointed by an association of which he may or may not be a member.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a very difficult thing to get down to individual cases. I do not agree with my hon. friend in his argument that just because a soldier, in the opinion of the board and consequently in the opinion of the minister, has not a good case, he should not be given any facilities to reach the court or the judge or the committee.
I am not going to argue that far.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
believe we would get very far with that sort of thing, but I am going to leave it for the moment. If you leave the matter to the judge, you will have the condition of affairs pictured by my hon. friend, of counsel appearing for the government and counsel appearing for the soldier. What does this mean? It means a hard and fast trial before a judge, settled on a point of law.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
think anyone can refute that. It means that and nothing else.

It could not possibly be
settled on a point of law; it would be settled
on a point of fact-the fact of value. The minister misunderstands the meaning of the phrase " a point of law."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite ready to be corrected on points of law as I am a layman, but I will challenge any of my legal friends to prove to me that an investigation held with the judge sitting as chairman of the board will not be less expensive and will not entail less legal array on both sides of the case. It will be rather a case of arbitration, because that is the name of the committee, the soldier coming before them if he so wishes. I cannot speak for all the provinces of Canada, but I can speak for my own province where the judge goes around to the smaller centres and holds his court. There is no reason why the committee cannot travel to those small centres and thus make it cheaper for the soldier to appear and bring his witnesses, lessening the cost, instead of having the cold and hard factor of law, which the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) speaks of, brought out before a county court judge. If you have lawyers 
there-and I do not say you can keep them out-I am going to say to my hon. friend that it will be hard for the soldier.

Why does my hon. friend press that point? Has he heard me suggest that there should be any lawyers there? I asked him what the policy of the department was to be as to pressing their side of the case and 1 gathered from what he said that they are going to have somebody there. If he wants to provide against lawyers appearing, let him say if he likes that the case be heard without lawyers. I am a lawyer, but I am willing to have it that way. I cannot understand how the minister thinks it is going to cost less to hear a case before three people, one of whom is the county court judge, than to hear it before the judge alone. The minister and I are old friends. He comes from within a few miles of where I live and I remember the highly judicial attitude he used to display in years gone by in the county of Simcoe. I know he knows something about law; he was even an assessor in his own township years ago and he learned something about municipal law. He is not green at all; he is a man of excellent judgment. But why does the minister introduce that point? How is any lawyer going to be involved in this? There is one question alone and that is the value of the land. The question of law does not and cannot arise. The question is purely as to whether you are going to have one or three men to say what the value of the land is. Perhaps I have interrupted the minister too soon and he may have some other arguments. I may say to him frankly that he has not advanced a solitary argument so far as I am concerned-and my mind is open- to show me that he is going to get any good results or save one cent by the process he has adopted as against the one advocated. Anyone who has any independent thought must see that a committee is going to lead to delay. The minister speaks about the tribunal moving about. Is it not easier and less expensive for a tribunal of one to go to the locality in which the land is than for a tribunal of three to go there? How can there be a saving of expense by having three on the committee? I know many people say that the district judges have not enough to do, but I do not subscribe to that. Some of them may not have as much as they can attend to, but many of them to my knowledge have a good deal to do. At the same time, however, I do not think that they have so much on their hands as to be unable to undertake this work as well. I think un-

Soldier Settlement Act
doubtedly that the district judge should do in this matter as is done in the divisional courts throughout the countiy: he should hold bis court in the place most convenient to the soldier and to the witnesses who would have to attend the trial. And the judge himself could go to that place, more conveniently and at less expense than could a tribunal of three. Perhaps I interrupted the minister too prematurely. In that case I still await with interest the 'convincing arguments that are to come to show why a tribunal of three will be less expensive and more practicable than a tribunal of one, that one being an independent judicial officer.
Does the minister say that if the judge is the sole arbitrator then the department proposes to be represented by a lawyer on each of these arbitrations?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that.

But that if, on the other hand, the tribunal is to consist of three, composed of the judge and two others representing the board and the soldier, the department does not intend to engage a lawyer? That is the inference that must be drawn from the minister's remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friends know that many of the representatives of the board are lawyers who naturally are better able to protect the interests of the board than a non-professional man could.
That would be hard on the soldier, who in such a case would have a lawyer against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I admit that at once, but I would point out to my hon. friend that the representative of the board, whether a lawyer or a layman, would undoubtedly have considerable experience in any case. He is dealing with these matters every day and is quite familiar with them. He knows the values of the lands and he can put up arguments to support his case, arguments which the soldier who is busily engaged in working his land, no matter how clever he may be, is not in a position to dispute if he appears in his own behalf. I should expect a representative of the settlement board to be a man of standing and judgment, and one who would be able to see that the interests of the board were protected without injustice to the soldier himself. My hon. friend tells me that I have not advanced any argument. Well, the strongest argument I have to offer is this, that by adopting the
plan I have suggested, the proceedings will not have the cold judicial character of a court in which there is formal submission of evidence. My hon. friends will not agree with that.

Per se, is that a harmful
thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not
suggesting that it is harmful, but I am of the opinion that the proposal I have submitted will make for a lower cost in the long run.

Will the minister tell us how
it could possibly do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall try
to if my hon. friends will give me a chance and not too frequently interrupt the trend of my statements. My argument briefly, is this: you cannot conduct a court without the employment of certain legal machinery. At least, I have not seen it done except in the case of an assessment court before which I have appeared in defence of my own position. In that case the municipality was represented by a lawyer, and I spoke only through him. In nine cases out of ten in which facts were heard by a court my experience has been that the appellant was represented by a lawyer. I am convinced that appeals to the courts are expensive. This conclusion I have been forced to after an experience of some seven years, during which time I have frequently settled matters outside, sometimes giving away more than I thought I should have done in the interests of the municipality in order to keep expenses within bounds. For there is no doubt about its being an expensive matter. A number of soldiers who have spoken to me have suggested that in cases where the board and the soldier could agree the matter might be settled by arrangement and, if it were thought advisable, referred to a judge for review, the court being resorted to only in the event of a disagreement between the board and the soldier.
There is no use in arguing that the soldier will be saved any money by one course in preference to the other. He has to submit his claim for consideration, whether it be by a committee consisting of a representative of the board and himself, or by some other tribunal. In order to facilitate matters the board has prepared forms which the soldier can fill out giving all the particulars necessary for the consideration of his case. He makes an affidavit that to the best of his knowledge and belief the statement he submits is a correct report of the conditions under which he is trying to carry on his farming operations. The board, on the other hand, if it disagrees,
237S
Soldier Settlement Act

naturally prepares a counter statement showing why the man should not be given the consideration for which he asks. I must say that I do not see any necessity for the employment of legal representatives to act on behalf of either party. It seems to me that they might quietly go before the board, submit their case, and have the arbitration committee settle the matter. I do not, of course, suggest that the judge could not do the same thing, but I fail to see where any reduction in expenses could be effected. I repeat what I said a few moments ago, that to my mind the strongest argument in favour of the plan suggested is that it will make for a more satisfactory settlement. You will get a better judgment from the representatives as named in the amended bill than you will from the hard and fast adjudication of the court itself. I may be wrong, but that is my conviction.

The minister says that the
soldier makes his application and supports it with an affidavit, and that the department rejoins with another. Am I to infer that this is to be the method of determining the value of the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
That is what I thought. Well, then, is it not the intention that witnesses shall be called either before a judge or before a tribunal of three?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I hardly
think it will be necessary to call witnesses in many cases. There may be a few serious cases of dispute, but on the whole I do not think that witnesses will be necessary.

I warn the minister that if
he does not provide in the bill that the evidence shall be documentary in the form of affidavits, there is not the slightest doubt that expert witnesses will be called to give evidence as to the value of the land. If the minister does not intend that witnesses shall be called, he must make some provision in that respect. Now, the minister speaks of a hard and fast legal tribunal. But what is the difference between a county court judge sitting alone, and a county court judge sitting on a tribunal of three? Are you not going to have the same evidence, the same documents submitted, and the same degree of activity and pressure in either case? So far as that answer goes, therefore, it is of no weight. If the minister lays it down that the soldier shall present his case in the form of an affidavit and the department shall do the same, I do not think it makes much difference whether

the tribunal consists of three or one, except as regards the greater expense entailed in the larger body.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The appearance of the soldier would not be precluded. When the form has been duly filled out applying for consideration, it must be backed up by an affidavit.

I understand that. Then the
next step is the hearing of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The next
step, if the board is not in possession of the full information, will be to send someone on a visit of inspection to the farm. The information submitted to the board might not agree with the complete facts as disclosed by that visit. Of course, I am anticipating a good deal; I have not thought out the form of procedure precisely. The next step would be to estimate the value.

The minister surely does not
mean that that is the procedure under this legislation. The application is made, and the committee must meet and hear the case. The case can be heard in one or two ways: either documentary evidence alone is accepted or a date is fixed for the hearing of the parties. Now, I have not the slightest doubt that this is what is contemplated by the bill.
Mr. STEW'ART (Edmonton): I say frankly we could not think of precluding the submission of evidence.

Then if this stands in its
present form you have the three of them and the parties appear either with witnesses or with counsel. So you have the same procedure, but in one case before three men and in the other before a single arbitrator.

Mr. Chairman, I have
been trying to get your eye for some time. Apparently the legal lights would like to hold the attention of the committee all the time. I want to bring a little horse sense into this discussion. For my part, I want nothing to do with the county judge. I do not want him on the bench either as a judge or in an advisory capacity. I want to see the soldier settler represented on that committee by one of his own number off the land. With all due respect to my legal friends, why should we select the county judge to the exclusion of the man on the land? If the minister will provide a small fee to bring the soldier from his district before the board, it will meet with my approval. I think I have more returned men in my constituency than has any other member.

Soldier Settlement Act
Question.

I think my friends will
find that I have as many returned men in my constituency as they have in theirs. I have had petitions from the men themselves, and they have asked to be allowed a representative on the board. As their member, it is only fair that I should ask that for them. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) says there will be no more Conservative members from Manitoba after the next general election because the Progressives and the Liberals are united and have got horse sense. He may be correct. Anyway, I am not playing politics in this. I only want to play the *game fair. I think the minister has a bill which meets with the approval of the returned men and of the soldier settlers on the land, who are asking for redress, for some assistance in the way of revaluation. During my campaign I met many of them, and I found they were all struggling grimly to hold on. After being three or four years at the front they were anxious to re-establish themselves on the land, but they were too keen and took their land at an exorbitant price. Now it is only fair to re-value that 'land and give those men a chance. Let me say to the minister in an advisory way:	Help the men, the men that
left their land for a few months or during last summer, help them to get back. Help them to get into live stock, and have a practical man travel through the country to teach those men how to carry on with mixed farming. The bill in my opinion meets with the approval of the returned men in Marquette.

Mr. Chairman, I heartily endorse what has been said by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) with respect to the clause now under consideration. There may be other clauses that I do not agree with, but I will deal with them when they are before the House. I am in favour of having a committee appointed as provided by the bill. I am not favourable to having a trial, as it were, of a judicial character before which the returned men must come in order to prove their case as to revaluation. I believe the soldiers themselves would be opposed to such a scheme and would rather favour the present arrangement. I do not believe it would cost as much as if they were compelled to go before a county judge. It would be necessary in a case of that kind, as the minister states, to have legal advice, because as laymen we do not favour court proceedings very much and we are not anxious to get into court more often than we have to. Consequently I believe the soldiers themselves favour the arrangement provided for
in this clause. I am not looking at it from the political point of view, I am considering it from the angle of the soldier settler who wishes for a revaluation of his land. I certainly approve of this section as brought down by the minister.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I have two questions to ask the minister. First, has he received representations from soldiers individually or from soldier organizations as to the manner in which they prefer to have the revaluation made? Second, with regard to this clause:
The minister may appoint district arbitration committees having jurisdiction in such soldier .settlement districts as may be necessary, eaoh committee to consist of three members, one of whom shall be the judge of the county or district court, as the case may be, of the county or judicial district within which the land is situate, such judge to be the chairman of the committee, one a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, and one a representative of a veterans' or settlers' organization in the district.
Is the minister to appoint the representative of the soldier's organization on his own initiative, or will he do so on the recommendation of the soldier's organization itself? That is a very important point. If the soldiers themselves, through their organization in the district, choose their representative, then I do not think there can be any objection, but if the minister appoints the representative arbitrarily then I think there is room for criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
had no representations from soldier organizations.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Or individually?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I have had nothing from soldiers individually. I have not had the opportunity of presenting this matter to them, I have been taking the consensus of opinion of hon. members with respect to the method to be pursued. As to the appointment of the representative of the soldiers, undoubtedly there will be some difficulty, as pointed out by my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) in judicial districts in British Columbia, for instance, where owing to the mountainous nature of the country the soldier settlements are not in such close communication with one another as they are on the prairies, and consequently difficulty might arise in the various communities not being able to agree upon a representative. But I may say to my hon. friend that I propose to accept the nominee of the soldiers' organization for the third member of the board.

Which organization?
Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have
named two. If there is an organization in existence,, we can accept the representative from that organization. If there is not any existence, there is nothing in the world to prevent the soldier settlers interested getting together and naming a representative.
But you may have a number of these organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I realize
that and admit frankly the difficulty so far as British Columbia is concerned. My hope was that the one representative would serve for the judicial district, but I am given to understand that that difficulty does exist in British Columbia.

Whose advice would
the minister take?

I think the minister is a
little in error as to the trial, as he calls it, which may occur before a judge. Would the minister remember that the reason he is putting a judge on this board is because of the experience any man on the bench gets in adjusting belief as to matters of fact, as well as of his knowledge of law. A very important quality of a judge is his ability to adjust conflicting questions of fact and get at the truth. May I also point out to the minister that a board of arbitration consisting of three members is in practice a farce. One party appoints one member; the other party appoints another, and the third member of the arbitration is appointed in some other way. The result is that the third man is the final adjudicator; the other two are counsel. Are we to have that sort of a board with one member, in effect, sitting for each party, and back of them again lawyers for the parties? I merely suggest to the minister that he is complicating matters by having a three-man board. It would be much more simple to create a one-man board.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
agree with my hon. friend.
