Then I think that is about the end of this discussion, so far as it goes, and I would like to get on to some point about which there is some opportunity for discussion. I think the House has covered this point pretty well, and if my hon. friend makes that his decision, I do not think we are usefully occupying our time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
wish to take issue with anyone in respect to his views, but I cannot help thinking that the two hon. gentlemen on the other side of the 
House (Mr. Mullins and Mr. Hay) have perhaps touched the vital point in this matter. I have no personal objection to a judge, I may say frankly, but I have reached the point in my own mind, judging from the arguments presented in this House

and I very frankly confess that I have not asked for outside opinion-where I think all parties will be better satisfied with the tribunal as provided for in the act than they would with the judge acting alone. That is my conviction at the moment, and of course one must stand by his convictions. I would be the last to criticize our judicial tribunals; I think our duty is to sustain them whether we like their decisions or not, but I do feel that in this as in many other cases where the judge is made chairman of the board, he will have some control over the committee, but after all it will not be a judicial hearing in the real sense of the term-

It never is; it could not
be.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -but will rather tend to give all parties a fair opportunity-

I would like to get some assurance from the minister that he will give the soldier some protection. Parliament is now trying to redress an injustice 5 p.m. done the soldier when he was sold land at inflated prices. I do not see how the soldier is going to profit very much by this court, or call it what you will, unless there is some provision whereby his case will be properly presented. That means that the government must get behind him with a certain amount of money. If the government does not do that the case of the soldier will not be properly presented and he will not in the end get justice. It seems to me that this is the important question in this whole undertaking. The soldier should and must have the right to select his own counsel, and that counsel should be paid by the department. Presumably the soldier has a credit balance in this country; if he has not a credit balance, due to his war service, this bill has no right to be before parliament. A part of that balance should be used in pressing his claims and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that unless the government makes some provision whereby he can obtain a certain amount of money by means of which his case may be properly presented, he may not get justice.
I am not reflecting on the good intentions of the government, nor on the purposes of the bill; it makes very little difference to me

Soldier Settlement Act
whether you have a one-man tribunal or a three-man tribunal; the soldier will likely get justice in either case if his case is properly presented. I would like the minister to give some assurance that his department will place a reasonable sum of money to the credit of the soldier in order to allow him to select his own counsel for the presentation of his case. If I were a soldier I would want a lawyer-and a good one-to present my case, and I think the more ably it is presented the more success he will have.

May I ask
one question? I understand that there are about 10,000 cases which would be affected by this legislation; there are probably 15,000 men who would make application for revaluation. Would the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat give us some idea of the expense his proposal would entail?

I am not concerned
with the expense; all I am concerned with is that justice be done to these men, and if this bill is not intended for that purpose it has no place before us.
We are all trying to do that, but this idea seems to me rather impractical.

Now that we have agreed
that there must be a revaluation it becomes a very important question as to what tribunal shall undertake this task. There is a good deal of truth in the old saying that the best committee is a committee of three with two members absent, and there is a good deal to be said for the contention that the county court judge should act in this capacity. I think, however^ that it might be just as *'veil for us to recognize the fact that the ordinary individual has some little suspicion of courts of justice. I do not share in the prejudice against judges and lawyers, but I think perhaps we should recognize that it does exist, and it seems to me that a court constituted under the terms of this bill would make a greater appeal to the men who are directly affected than would a county court judge acting alone. It might be well to point out that the right hon. leader of the opposition took the ground that there was some danger that the interests of the country might be jeopardized, and that the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board-who might be spoken of as the representative of the government-would be likely to sacrifice the interests of the government. On the other hand the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) took the stand that it would not be fair to the soldier to have this board
constituted as this act provides. Those two gentlemen drew two different conclusions from the same premises.
I think there is also a misapprehension as to the spirit in which this tribunal is likely to deal with these matters. I do not anticipate that it will be in the nature of a hard and fast legal trial, or a board of arbitration in which the representative of each party to the dispute is trying to get something excessive for those whom he represents. Naturally, of course, the soldier in the case will want to get his land revalued at the lowest possible figure, but, I do not anticipate that the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board will try on the other hand to secure the utmost he could possibly get from that tribunal. I anticipate that the attitude of the Soldier Settlement Board will be that a large measure of reduction in most cases is necessary, and instead of taking the attitude that it will get the highest possible value placed upon the land_ it will meet the soldier settler in the spirit of give and take and try to arrive at an amicable decision.
Now as regards the matter of expenditures. It is to be expected, of course, that a tribunal of three will be a little more expensive than a tribunal of one. But in regard to the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board I think it might be pointed out that the board will have one representative there anyway-there can bn no question of that-and the representative of that board who must be on the tribunal will furnish it with all the information the board has at its disposal and thus it will be placed in possession of all the facts of the case. Naturally during all these years through which the board has been operating it has become possessed of a great deal of detailed information. I know you can go to that board to-day and get detailed information in regard to any given case. In the very nature of the case the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board will be. furnished with that information when he comes to take part in the proceedings of this arbitration. Therefore I cannot understand why there should be necessity for any other lawyer in the case at all. It seems to me there should be no necessity for any other lawyer to present the case because the representative of the board will be in possession of all the information which the board has to offer upon the subject.
Mr. McGIBB'ON:	Put yourself in the
soldier settler's place. Would you not want to see your case presented in the most favourable light before the board?
Soldier Settlement Act

Up to the present I have
not discussed the matter from the soldier settler's standpoint. If the hon. member will wait perhaps I will come to that. I have been discussing the matter so far only from the standpoint of the board. I say naturally that the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board will be in possession of all the facts the board has to offer upon the matter.
Now let us come to the standpoint of the soldier settler. Naturally he would wish to be represented or to appear in person before the tribunal, and many of these soldier settlers are themselves thoroughly competent men, able to argue their own case, and to make the most effective presentation of it. Therefore, in a great many instances they would not require the services of counsel at all. On the other hand I quite understand that many men are in such a position that it would be very desirable that they should have counsel. In such cases I think it would be quite proper that the government should make provision for the satisfactory presentation of the soldier's case. I would agree heartily with that, knowing as I do that perhaps many men might not be able to look after their own interests if they were not properly advised. Putting one method over against the other-taking the judge on the one hand and the tribunal as provided for in the bill on the other-while there is something to be said in favour of the judge alone acting, it seems to me that taking everything into consideration greater satisfaction will be given by the provisions of the bill to the men whose interests are directly affected, rather than by allowing them to go before a county court judge acting alone, notwithstanding, I admit, that from the standpoint of strict logic a good deal may be said for the position of those who represent that the county court judge alone should act.

I would suggest to the
minister that in the great majority of cases when application is made for a reduction in the value of land the soldier settler has a representative at hand, the local representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, who has been in touch with each and every one of these cases for years back. Why could it not be arranged that a settlement should be made, if possible, as between that representative and the soldier settler, and only those cases referred to the arbitration committee or to the judge where such a settlement was not possible? If necessary we could safeguard that by saying that settlements so made, if any, should be referred for final decision to the judge who is to be the head of the arbitration board. I am quite satisfied in my own mind that the man who has been in touch with the settler, who knows 
the actual conditions, the value of the land- if his experience is worth anything he should know the actual value of the land at the present time-and the circumstances under which each of these settlers purchased his land, is competent to act, and if such an arrangement could be made between the two parties, that is between this local man as representing the government and the soldier-settler, there is no need for any abitration or for any proceedings other than, perhaps, a, review of the finding before the county court judge. In that way we would obviate the questions that arise this afternoon.
I would further say that I am in favour of the one-man tribunal. I think the judge is all that is necessary in these cases. In the great majority of instances the local county court judge is pretty well in touch with the conditions as to farm lands and everything, else within his own jurisdiction. So I say that one man would be just as good as three. I believe it is quite possible in the case of sixty or seventy per cent of these cases, perhaps more, to effect a settlement without any trouble at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I may say
that was what was contemplated by the bill' as originally drafted, but changes were made in order to meet the varied arguments in the House. May I answer my hon. friend at once by saying that where the parties are in agreement the appearance before the arbitration board will be purely perfunctory.
The bill does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will be the procedure; as a matter of fact, it cannot be otherwise. My hon. friend suggested that there should be a review -of the decision. In such cases there will be a review, that is where the Soldier Settlement Board and the settler agree. That is why I provide the tribunal; so that there shall be a final and complete settlement. In such cases, the preliminaries, such as those my hon. friend suggested, having been gone through and the parties being in agreement, it is only a matter of obtaining sanction; there will be no necessity even for the soldier to appear on his own behalf.
That would not appear to be the case from the provisions of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The act
does not so provide, it is true, but it is the procedure that will be followed.

Even though I do not look at the matter exactly from the same angle as my right hon. friend, the leader of the-

Soldier Settlement Act
opposition, I am in entire accord with him that this tribunal should be composed of one judge only, the county court judge. In order that hon. members may be correctly seized of the situation I should like to go back and recall the principles on which this legislation was founded. The right hon. leader of the opposition will recall that this act was not conceived with the object of helping the returned soldiers. It was conceived purely and simply as a colonization scheme. In order to show that this theory is the right one I have only to recall to the memory of those who were in the House in 1920 and 1921 the efforts made by hon. members to induce the government of that day to help the returned soldiers who were in other walks of life than agriculture. On many occasions members asked that mechanics be assisted, tnat small shopkeepers be assisted, and they said, "If you help the farmers, why not help the others?" Invariably the answer came back "We are rendering assistance to returned soldiers to place them on the land because they are the best settlers, and this is purely and simply a colonization scheme and not a scheme to help returned men." That being the case, let us see what has happened? We have squandered something like eighty to a hundred million dollars on a scheme that was badly conceived, badly administered, apd which we now find is bankrupt. Therefore the best thing to do is to get out of it as cheaply as we can. I therefore suggest that we appoint one judge on the tribunal, because a judge would be neither trammelled by the exigencies of the returned soldier, nor influenced by the amiability possibly cf some member of the Settlement Board who might be only too willing to assist the returned soldier to help himself. A soldier in such a case might get far more than he was entitled to. Therefore, in the interests of the country, in order to rescue the country from the deplorable situation in which it was placed when this scheme was put in force, I suggest that one judge be appointed, and, in spite of what the hon. minister has said, that he give not a hard and fast legal judgment, but a decision as fair as possible and one through which the country may suffer the least possible.

In common with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I believe that having arrived at the decision to assist the soldier on the land, the matter to be determined is, what is the best way to do it? Clause (e) provides that the minister may appoint a district arbitration committee
and he chooses as the first member the county judge; then he selects a member of the Soldier Settlement Board and then he selects a third-the minister, not the soldier-and the third may be a member of the veterans' or settlers' organization. Where is the soldier represented on that board? The minister selects those three or one of them is selected by the state, and he is the county court judge. The other two are selected by the minister. The soldier is not represented unless he secures counsel to represent him, and when he is going before that board he is going before two men who are representing the state and his dispute, if he has a dispute, is with the state; we may call it the Soldier Settlement Board if we will, but- in reality they represent the state, and the other arbitrator, selected by the minister from some of the soldiers' organizations, if there happen to be such, is also a representative of the state. These two agree, and where does the district court judge come in?
If the minister would leave that matter in the hands of the district court judge then, the money he is going to spend could be saved, Let the Soldier Settlement Board be represented by someone appointed by the state, and let the third man, the soldier's representative, who need not necessarily be a lawyer, be selected by the soldier himself. If he wishes to select him from the soldiers' organization where there happens to be one,, well and good. If he desires to secure a farmer residing on the next farm to him, let that farmer be his representative, but let him be the representative of the soldier.
Coming to the matter of securing the representative from the soldiers' organization, the question has been asked, what organization are you going to select him from? I know one judicial district in this country where there are two distinct soldier organizations. There was what was formerly the Great War Veterans' organization and there is a complete and separate organization now, quite apart from that organization, and refusing to recognize it, and it is termed the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. I know another district where there is no such soldiers" organization. What are you going to do in that case? Take the newer parts of the country where the settlers are far apart, we find the soldiers are sparsely distributed. There may be twenty-five miles between one soldier and another, and then there may be two or three in a group. (Where will you get the soldiers' organization to represent these men?' You cannot get one. But they have just the same right to representation as the soldier re-
Soldier Settlement Act

siding in a district where there are a thousand soldiers. If this measure is to be made effective and satisfactory to the settler, make it as simple as you can, leave it to the district court, let the minister put in a provision by which the Soldier Settlement Board will present the case for the soldier, let the soldier select a man to present his case, and let the department pay for it and fix the fee now. Do not make it possible to have these legal gentlemen getting the large fees that have been spoken of. Set a reasonable per diem allowance. A practical, experienced farmer, if you will, might be selected by the soldier settler to present the case to the tribunal if the soldier so desires. If the soldier desires a lawyer, fix the same per diem for the lawyer as for the farmer, and if the lawyer does not take it somebody else will. Simplify it, let three men comprise the tribunal, but do not have a board with two representatives of the state, or a board the members of which are all selected by the minister and the government, because this would leave the matter in the hands of the government itself to dispense justice as it saw fit.

Has the government a
policy or plan worked out by which it purposes to revalue the land for its own information? Naturally when the representatives go before the committee they must have a very definite idea themselves as to the value of the land. I presume the government has some policy under which the value is to be arrived at.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In all cases where that information is not already in the possession of the board it will be necessary for them to make an appraisal of the property, having in mind of course the provisions of clause (c) in the act. They will consider what in their opinion the value of the land is at the present day and make their representations accordingly. The soldier, also having in mind what he has to do, would make his representations from the same basis. Now they may or may not agree, but that would be the ordinary method of establishing the value for assessment purposes or anything else. That is just the method to be pursued, and one must bear in mind that in both cases we are subject to the human frailties of the individual who makes the valuation.

The valuation would
be made by the local officer of the board. I should like to point out to the minister some confusion that would arise in that way. Each man would have different ideas as to the value, and I think it would be important

that one set of possibly exceptionally well qualified appraisers should be appointed, and re-value all that- land in respect to which application for reduction is made. Then you would have at least standardization. In one particular district the officer might have an opinion as to the value of the land quite different from that of the officer operating in the next district. When you come before the appeal board you will have the case cited in one of the districts where the land is valued low, and it will be presented as an argument in favour of reduced value in another district; so that if you get a regular man appointed who would re-value all the land, it seems to me you would eliminate a lot of trouble. I can see no reasonable argument in favour of submitting all this to a judge. I believe that in ninety per cent and possibly more of the cases, the revaluation would be worked out quite satisfactorily between the board and the soldiers themselves. If we have confidence in the Soldier Settlement Board to administer the business they have to administer to-day. surely they are qualified to carry this out, and if we have not confidence in them, it is time we got another board. I do not see any good reason for submitting this to a judge.
The argument has been raised that politics will work into it. Politics works into every department of government to a degree, but when there are only 17,000 soldiers, even if every single	one	of them	were put in aposition where he practically had to support the government, that would not keep any government in power. As an opponent of the government I	would not be very greatly	concerned about	that	angle of	the matter,	andin any case	the	question	of loss to	the
treasury is not so great as it would appear because if, through favouritism, some soldier got a particularly low valuation, neighbouring soldiers would naturally use that in the appeal as an argument for revaluation of their lands. Therefore, I cannot conceive of the board going to any great degree in extending favouritism to any soldier. I do not think they could get away with it. The revaluation must be worked out on a reasonable and equitable basis. Naturally, these soldiers will all be watching one another in order to see what the revaluation of their respective land is. If one of these men, because he might be a political favourite, got a large amount written off his debt, naturally the other men would have an argument in asking for the same treatment.

speechtext: No. Because the officers of the government have no power in the world to make concessions to soldiers to-day. The act will not permit them to do so. It never followed such a principle.

They have considerable
power to make concessions in granting loans. In one particular case I have in mind, the granting of seed grain to soldiers who lost their crops, they have great power and I have never seen it abused. I think they have used very good judgment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Granting loans which the fellow has to pay-of course that has to pass through quite a number of imprimaturs before it is finally done. There is really no opportunity there. The great thing is that the man has to pay it.
If the land is overvalued, naturally he will not be able to pay it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not now, but he felt he had to when he got the money, and it was not any great benefit to him to get more than he could pay back. In the original act the opportunities for fraud were undoubtedly reduced to the very minimum. It was made a criminal offence to take any commission, for example, on a sale. In the purchase of land the soldier himself had to select it, be satisfied with it, be content with the price, and so declare over his signature to the board. Those were two precautions. In the next place the soldier could not gain anything by pajung too much; he had everything to lose Next, the Farm Loans Board had to be satisfied; before fraud could creep in they had to be deceived or they had to be dishonest 14011-152
Next, the inspector had to be satisfied; before fraud could creep in he had to be deceived or he had to be dishonest. I think the House will admit that there were a series of fortifications against fraud on the treasury which were at least as great as they could be made, but the House knows that they were not successful. The House knows that fraud was committed over top of the whole of them; that the rapacious man got in, got his fist on the treasury and got away with it. He did this to quite an extent on the west shore of lake Manitoba. All these men who should have been on guard were put into a moral sleep; one after another was deceived or one after another was fraudulent. This was the case east of lake Winnipeg as well. As I said before the cases were not general; they were isolated and the proportion was small. Nevertheless, the amount was large and! it was the cause of the worst situation we have in the whole field of soldier settlement.
What is going to be the opportunity in this case? I remind the minister again that he is going to allow the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board and the man to make an arrangement which nobody in the world can upset, which is final. I remind the minister too that while the judge might have power to speak and to advise, that is all the power he has and knowing that, nine out of ten of them will never say a word if the Soldier Settlement Board and the man agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely the
right hon. member is not suggesting that the judge would sit quiet under what he considered was a fraud committed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How does he know it to be a fraud? The two come before him. The soldier says that the land is worth so much and the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board agrees. The judge knows nothing about it. There are no witnesses. In nineteen cases oult of twenty they will just put their O.K. right there. Like other people they are not running about the country trying to put more work on their backs.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely some uniformity would be preserved. I think one hon. gentleman who spoke from the Progressive party put his finger on the spot. I admit that you cannot frame any statute under which you can protect the country against fraud, but as in the case . of assessment appeals consideration is had to the surrounding property and it must be so in every case. The judge is the man who perhaps knows as much as anybody about that, because it is part of his official duty, and I cannot conceive

Soldier Settlement Act

that he would sit still under what would appear to be a fraudulent readjustment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How would it appear to be so? There would be nothing to appear at all. The judge has nothing before him but blank space. He does not know a thing about the matter. I will venture to say that in nineteen cases out of twenty, if not in ninety-nine out of a hundred, the judge would never have seen that special piece of land with the idea of coming to any estimate of its value.
The minister says there must be some uniformity, and the hon. member for Mackenzie mentioned it. I do not know where there is any uniformity in land values. I have quite a little land and I do not know two quarter sections that are uniform in any degree. Imagine such a thing as uniformity in farm land values! There are a dozen considerations in regard to lands that are immediately adjoining, one across the road from the other. Five hundred dollars would be a small variation between one farm on one side of the road and another on the other side, although perhaps both looked the same from the road. That would be accounted for by some characterization of the soil, by the lay of the land. The minister is going to have to use hundreds of representatives of that board. He has to do it. These representatives, I will assume, are of average honesty; they have done their work well and they have the confidence of the board. But they have never had anything in the world to do that would enable them to make money illegitimately. Here, however, that oportunity is going to be put in their way. The $500 could be divided between somebody and the representative and they could go before the judge and agree on the valuation. Who is ever going to find it out? Where is the precaution? There is none at all. The minister is really opening the door of the treasury. That is what he is doing. He is not doing it intentionally, but the fact is that he has not provided himself with a single fortification. And if he remembers his Horace he knows that the immortal greed of gold will tempt the heart of man to do nearly anything. Why should we expose ourselves in this way? There is no need of it. The representative of the Soldier Settlement Board and the soldier should not be given the right to come to a decision not subject to review by anybody. The principle cannot be defended at all and the minister will regret the day he ever suggested it to this House. I have nothing to say about the motives of anyone, but I do say no one has ever sought to administer so vast a thing as this in such a way.
Will not the danger be just as great where the two parties agree to a certain decision before going to the judge?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is precisely the
danger against which I have been arguing ever since the subject came up. My contention is that the representative of the board and the soldier should never be allowed to come to an agreement. To allow them to do so is to open wide the door to fraud to the extent of millions.
Is there then no means by which a plaintiff and a defendant could agree between themselves?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is neither plaintiff nor defendant in this case. The man who is supposed to represent the government is protecting not his own money but the country's. For that reason the principle of plaintiff and defendant does not apply here. That is why an exchequer court is necessary. I suggest that in every case the two should go before the judge and have the judge himself send for the witnesses, the responsibility resting upon him finally. He should decide as to the value of the land. The judge should be held responsible. He will probably spend the rest of his life in the community and his reputation depends upon the honesty of his work. But what about the others? They would likely be gone the next day and no one would know anything about the matter. I appeal to the minister and those behind him not to expose the country to such a peril.

Some machinery should be provided in relation to the appointment of the representative of the soldier or settler. The bill as it stands before us does not make that point clear at all. If I followed the minister I inferred that one man would act for the settlers in the whole of the judicial district. How will he be appointed and from whom is the minister going to accept advice in that appointment? In my constituency there are a number of soldier organizations-the Army and Navy, the Great IVar Veterans, the Imperial Veterans, and now a new organization, the Canadian Legion. The bill speaks of "a representative of the veterans' or settlers' organization." In my opinion something will have to be incorporated in the bill to clear up this point; otherwise there will be a good deal of trouble. There is nothing here to provide for the returned men in the district getting together and agreeing upon a man to represent them. I want to hear the minister's view on the question. We should know just how the appointment is to be made.

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I admit the difficulty and I say frankly that the responsibility is one that I do not like. Unfortunately, however, I do not know of any way of avoiding it and of deciding what representative shall act on behalf of the soldier settler.
I should prefer a representative from amongst the soldier organizations themselves rather than from an organization outside, which might not be particularly interested in the soldier settlement scheme. I would say however that someone representing as nearly as possible the men themselves should be selected, named by them and not 'by me.

The minister says that he would like to get rid of the responsibility of making this selection. There is a simple way by which he may do so, and that is pot to have this provision in the bill at all. There is nothing here that provides that the soldiers' organization shall appoint the representative, or that the soldier will have anything to do with that appointment. The simple fact is, as my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) has pointed out, that two men will settle the matter between themselves before going to the judge. If the minister wants to escape the undesirable position which he has indicated, I suggest that he have nothing to do with the appointment of the representative, but allow the soldier to select his own man, the government paying that man whatever they would have to pay an arbitrator. I do not think they could get anybody to act for nothing. Let the representative of the board and the representative of the soldier present the case to the judge and let the judge take the full responsibility. That would relieve the minister and the Soldier Settlement Board of any possibility not only of embarrassment but ultimately of wrongdoing.

There are too many
technicalities in this bill. The government is providing for a tribunal which is to be rigged up after the fashion of a high court of justice. We know that you create here the same machinery as is used to take over a railway or public corporation worth millions, namely, an arbitration court of a judge and two arbitrators with him. Why should such ridiculous procedure be followed here as in connection with street railways, where merely a few acres of land are involved? The cost of this matter is going to come out of the soldiers in the long run, and the trouble with all soldier legislation in this country is that 14011-152J
it- is not practical enough. Some 100,000 of our returned soldiers have had to go to the United States to look for work, while about
17,000	have been game enough to go upon the land in Canada, and those who have done so have had considerable hardships to endure, requiring the exercise of human qualities of endurance, courage, resource, skill, perseverance that are more the qualities of a race than an individual. This country has given away millions of acres of land to our railways; yet finds it almost impossible to take care adequately of the soldiers who went overseas and fought for us. We are here setting up all the red tape of a superior court of justice in connection with this matter, with all the attending cost and lack of results. Where does the soldier and his family come in while all this red tape is going on? These men demand practical soldier legislation and not technicalities after the Pension Board fiasco. Have we no time to deal with questions affecting our returned men? Are we to devote our time wholly to debating technical points respecting the most impracticable bill that could be introduced on behalf of the men who so nobly did their duty for the empire? I appreciate the difficulties of the minister, but why not put the onus on the county court judges or quaei-judicial officers? Or why not appoint a federal commission of several specially well qualified commissioners to deal with this very important work. Let such a commission take up the whole problem affecting the 17,000 cases involved and get quick action. A similar course was taken in connection with the Home Bank depositors, and I see no reason why a royal commission should not be appointed to deal with what is of vital importance to our returned men.
I urge the minister to adopt this course. Let us quit fooling with this problem-appoint several judicial commissioners to settle these claims quickly, cut out petty matters and settle the bill.

Mr. 'Chairman, in dealing with the personnel of the board, I think the suggestion of my right hon. leader is the proper one to adopt. There seems to be some misconception by hon. members as to what that suggestion involves. What was in the mind of my right hon. leader when he suggested this machinery was that the county court judge should act independently as a kind of valuator, that he should obtain evidence as to the value of the land and decide what that

value really should be. Now, our district or county court judges are thoroughly conversant with land values. Members who state the contrary are perhaps unaware of the fact that those judges are continually dealing with actions for foreclosure of mortgages and for specific performance of agreements of sale of real estate, all involving valuation of land. This is simply a matter of precisely the same kind and nature. However, if the minister is absolutely determined to have a board of arbitration, then, inasmuch as he has stated that he is anxious to withdraw as far as possible from all responsibility of appointing the members of such boards, I think he should tell us just how he proposes that the appointments should be made. Difficulties have been raised by members who are familiar with conditions in some of the ridings, and who know that the bill in its present form is utterly impracticable. The minister, I take it, admits that as the bill reads he himself has the absolute right of appointment of all members of the board of three. He says he is anxious to get away from that responsibility-

I wish now to direct the minister's attention to two other points. To one of them I referred when the bill first came before the House. Subsection (a) of section 1 of the bill reads as follows:
Application for revaluation can be considered only when made by a settler residing on and himself farming the said land.
I called the attention of the minister to the fact that there might be instances-and I understand from some members on this side that this is more than a mere supposititious case; that there are in point of fact cases- where soldiers who have current agreements of sale with the Soldier Settlement Board which are not in default, or which at any rate have not been determined through default, may not be personally farming the land. For some reason or other they may have someone farming it for them, or may have leased the land to a tenant. speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 17-Hon. Mr. Stewart- to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919, Mr. Duff in the chair.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was dealing with sub-section (a) of section 1, which addresses itself to the soldier settlers who are to come within the provisions of the bill, and I was urging on the minister the advisability of extending the provisions of the bill to embrace not merely soldier settlers who are personally in occupation of the lands and engaged in active farming operations on them, but also those soldier settlers who, possibly and probably for no reason over which they have control- being still purchasers under contracts in good standing, or contracts at any rate not yet determined by default of payment of the purchase money and ejectment-are not able at present to carry on farming operations. I told the committee that I had the assurance of one hon. member from Manitoba that I was not imagining such a case, that there were in fact cases of this kind. It is not open to the government, it is not open to the House, to make answer: parliament has the right to give all these gratuitous benefits to whomsoever it will. The Minister of the Interior used that argument in introducing the bill. He admitted that certain classes of soldier settlers who appeared to be legally, legitimately entitled to the benefits of the bid were being excluded, that no provision was being made for them. He frankly admitted that these provisions were being confined to one particular class, and the justification he suggested for that was this:	Owing to the deflation of land values,
private vendors continually make readjustments of prices and terms with their purchasers, who otherwise would throw back the lands on their hands, and the new sales no doubt would be at greatly diminished prices. And the argument seemed to be that inasmuch as the private vendor had a right to say whether he would make a new arrangement and abandon part of his purchase price, and had a right to say that he would make such concessions to certain purchasers and not make them to others, the Dominion government and the parliament of Canada had a right to do the same thing. In my humble opinion the argument of the

Soldier Settlement Act
Minister of the Interior is unsound, because one of his premisses is false. The parliament of Canada is not in the position of a private purchaser using his own money. The parlia* ment of Canada is using the money of the taxpayers of this country, using the money of the people of this country, and amongst the very people whose money is being used are these soldier settlers who are being left out of the purview of the bill.
Is that the argument of the Minister of the Interior or the leader of the opposition?

In my recollection it was the
argument of the Minister of the Interior, that these readjustments had continually to be made by private vendors because of the deflation in prices. Now if Canada as a country was in the position of a private vendor I would agree with the argument, because in that, case the Dominion would be using its own money and therefore would have the right to say whether it would or would not make a concession in respect to the money that was due to it-it would be its own money and the Dominion would be the only one to be hit and hurt. But here we are using the money of the people of Canada for concessions to certain soldier settlers, and that very money is the money of other soldier settlers as well as of other taxpayers. Therefore we are not in the same position as a private vendor. I do not see how you can possibly get away from that. You are doing an injustice to a certain class of soldier settlers, and they have the right-these soldier settlers whose claims are not being met, the men who have paid in full for their lands or the men who, by reason of the inflated prices which they paid for the land in the first instance, have made default in their payments and have been ejected, or the mep who have not yet' been ejected but are not personally farming for some reason or otliei-all these men, or any one of them, can come to the Parliament of Canada and say "You have made a concession to these soldier' settlers out of the funds of this country to which I contributed, and I have the same right as they have." I cannot see how the minister can get away from the fact that if the bill passes in its piesent form it will be an injustice to the soldier settlers who, it may be, have paid in lull, not merely out of the proceeds of the:r farms but possibly out of personal m mays that they had acquired from some other source, or which they borrowed and subsequently paid back. And
you will be doing an injustice to those soldier settlers who have not paid in full but who are not able ao present personally to continue farming operations.

Provided that in any case where the actual sale price is greater than the maximum amount which under section sixteen of this act may ibe advanced by the board in the purchase of land on behalf of any settler, such maximum amount shall be deemed the sale price for the purposes of this section.

:	Here is a provision of the
