speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is hardly correct. The hon. gentleman will notice that under section 17 there may be cases where $5,500 will be the maximum, or in exceptional cases it may go to $6,000, where the buildings are taken into consideration. But the point is this: the government are not taking into consideration any additional payments the soldier may have made, because I understand in some cases they have paid as high as $2,000. I presume the board took the view that if he were willing to make the investment, and he thought the property was worth that, that was really his business. Whether or not that was a proper position to take, I am not going to argue, but the fact remains that we are providing only for the amount of money invested in the property by the government itself.

The minister is not doing that. I thought that was what he intended to do, but what he says is this: Where a man has paid more than $5,000, say, $6,000, $7,000, $8,000, $9,000, $10,000 or as high as you like for his farm, the price for the purpose of valuation is to be taken as $5,000 and then there is deducted from that the new value put on the land. In other words, supposing the new valuation is $4,000, the concession is $1,000 and no more. As regards the statem'ent of the minister about section 17 or any other section in the act of 1919, the only section mentioned in the bill is section 16 and that is the only section with which we are concerned. I do not know whether the intention of the government now is that the bill should stand as it is. I had thought that probably the government's intention was in every case to take the amount at which the farm was valued by the Soldier Settlement Board for the purpose of the loan or the amount of money which the Soldier Settlement Board lent on the farm, and to make their deductions from that. But that is not what the bill says.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is arguing that we should take in every case the exact amount the government invested in the property?

I thought that was what the government intended to do.

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As nearly as possible. I want my hon. friend to realize how difficult it is to get that amount.

Yes. Those are the two
points I would like to call to the attention of the minister, because they are quite vital points.

Paragraph (e) reads:
Each committee to consist of three members, one of whom shall be the judge of the county or district court, as the case may be, of the county or judicial district which the land is situate, such judge to be the chairman of the committee, one a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, and one a representative of a veterans' or settlers' organization in the district.
Is it the intention of the minister to appoint that representative of the veterans' or settlers' organization in the district?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is the
intention of the government to accept the nominee preferably of the settlers themselves. One of the difficulties we meet with in getting a representative of the soldiers is that there are two or three different soldiers' organizations, but as the only soldier who is interested in this revaluation is the man on the land himself, we shall as far as possible deal with the nominee of the soldier settlers.

Will it be the soldier
settlers in the district that will make the appointment, or will it be the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They make the recommendation. I have to assume the responsibility of making the appointment.

That is putting too much leverage in the hands of the minister to make political appointments, and I do not agree with that. I want the minister to leave that out and to let the appoinment be made by the settlers in the district. They know more about the matter and it is only fair to them that they should make the appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no
objection in the world, but I want my hon. friend to understand how difficult that would be. I have no concern about the actual naming of the man, but if my hon. friend has had anything to do with soldiers' organizations, he knows how many of them there are and how bitterly they can disagree amongst themselves. That is the only reason on earth why the matter is being dealt with in this way. If there was one definite organization in each province and it would name a satisfactory man for each judicial district, I would accept such nomination at once. I have no desire to interfere. My sole desire would be to accept [Mr. Bury.)
the nominee of the organization that was really representative of the soldier settlers themselves.

I would be far more satisfied if the minister would agree to have the appointment made by the soldier settlers, so as to give them a chance to have some say in the matter without any political influence being brought to bear upon them.

I would like to recommend to the minister that he should have one of the soldiers' organizations either in the district or in the province nominate the men's representative who would sit on this committee.
I do not wish to delay the passage of the bill or to make an amendment to it, but I feel sure it would be more satisfactory to the soldier settlers if they had the right to nominate their representative on this committee. Can the minister see his way clear to amend the bill along this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will at once admit the difficulty. I canvassed the situation pretty thoroughly. In Alberta, which is perhaps representative of most of the provinces, we have two or three provincial organizations representative of returned soldiers. I doubt very much whether the soldier settler has much representation in any of those organizations, although they are provincial in character. They perform a splendid service for the man who has pension difficulties and all that sort of thing, but the soldier settler has been somewhat outside of that. If the soldier settlers would nominate amongst themselves in each judicial district one who would represent them, I would have no objection in the world to appointing him.

That is what I am asking, but the bill does not provide for that. The minister has said that he wishes to dissociate himself from the matter in a political way. I can understand his difficulty in getting soldier settlers to agree upon a man, because I do not suppose there are many active organizations in the country districts representing soldier settlers. I can understand the difficulty of the minister in that respect, but I submit that the matter should be taken from the sphere of political influence.

I am glad to note that the
minister sees the difficulty he is in.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Let me assure my hon. friend that I am not seeing it now for the first' time; I have appreciated that difficulty from the beginning.
Soldier Settlement Act

I am glad to note, however, that it is becoming more apparent. The situation is one that, in my opinion, was impossible when the bill was drafted, as it is impossible now. The minister declares that he is anxious to divorce himself from all responsibility in connection with these appointments but this very bill enacts that he himself shall be the person to make the appointments. The board will not be one of arbitration in the interests of the soldier, inasmuch as it will be nominated by the minister himself. No matter how anxiqus he may be to evade responsibility for the appointments, the minister can not do so if he insists upon this bill. He and no one else will nominate both the man who is to represent the board and the man who will represent the soldier. Furthermore, the minister will name the third independent arbitrator, the county court judge. Why not leave the soldier alone to look after his owrn interests instead of taking so paternal an interest in him as to nominate the man who is to represent him? I do suggest to the minister that he might very well leave the matter to the county court judge. The judge, I am sure, would not be wedded to formalities, and he would have no hesitation in accompany' ing the parties interested in the dispute on an inspection of the land, viewing it in order to arrive at a common sense decision. The county court judge would be independent both of the soldier and of the board. If the minister is sincerely desirous to get rid of the responsibility in this matter let him leave it to a member of the judiciary who by the very nature of his office would be independent of all concerned; and let the soldier name his own representative to take care of his interests in the arbitration. It is always possible, of course, for the soldier and the representative of the board to come to an agreement, but I can see no reason why the minister should not leave it solely to the judge to decide upon a fair valuation of the land when the representative of the board and the representative of the soldier come before him. These two might say that in their opinion the land should be valued at less than the price at which it was originally sold, and if the judge were not satisfied the responsibility would rest with him. If the judge were appointed there would be no possibility of collusion between the soldier and the representative of the board or anyone else, and there would be a greater likelihood of justice being done. If necessary the minister could make regulations requiring the judge to view the land and give a valuation where there was no dispute between the two representatives. In any case FMr. C. A. Stewart.]
we can rest assured that in every instance the judge would see that justice was done and that there was no opportunity for any sort of collusion. Only adopting that course can the minister divorce himself from the responsibility which apparently he is anxious to avoid; and only by that course can justice be done to the soldier.

When I point out that
personally I should be perfectly willing to accept the decision of the county court judge recently appointed in Hants-Kings, I am sure the minister will acquit me of any desire to be anything but absolutely fair to himself. I make that statement even though the gentleman to whom I refer was a late official of the Liberal party and a Liberal member of this House in the last parliament. I am sure that no one would have any hesitation about accepting any judgment he might render in a matter of this kind. If the minister has made up his mind to have a board of three, the language of the paragraph before us makes it clear that he himself or his successor, should he leave his present office, will have the responsibility of appointing the three. Now, let us suppose that there is a community in which there are five or six or, if you prefer, say two or three soldier organizations, meeting in their respective halls, and each appointing a candidate for the board. I pay the minister this compliment, from the short acquaintance that I have had with him, that if he remained in charge of the department I should be quite willing to trust to his selection of one man out of these five or six competitors. But there might be a change of ministers and one might not be quite so ready to depend upon the selection in that case. If the minister is not willing to admit that the county court judge is fit to be made the sole arbitrator, I would suggest that at least he amend the bill to provide that the judge and the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board should choose the soldiers' representative from among the rival candidates. By so doing the minister would relieve himself of responsibility, shifting it partly to the judge and partly to the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board.

Does the hon. member, or
any other hon. gentleman for that matter, know of any rural settlement that contains two, three, four or five rival soldier settler organizations?

Right at the moment I
cannot point to any case; I am frank with my hon. friend. But I can point to a number of returned soldiers who would not at

Soldier Settlement Act
all be willing to accept the nominee who might be selected by the soldier settlement club or league or other gathering in a certain community. If my hon. friend has not a similar situation in his own constituency, then I can assure him he is very well favoured indeed.
It may exist as to individuals but not as to organizations.

May I suggest to the
minister that he allow the soldier organization to select a member of the committee? I have a petition sent to me by seventeen soldier settlers in the vicinity of Marquette. I know every one of these boys; they were raised in the district and they are all absolutely capable of taking a seat on that committee. If he does not want to select them from the district, let him select them from the provincial organization. Either method will be satisfactory to the soldier settlers. I think it would be well for the minister to amend the clause to meet this objection. It seems to be the only objection to the bill. I would prefer to have one of the boys on the board independently of any appointment by the minister or the Soldier Settlement Board.

Mr. Chairman, I can
readily understand that the minister is somewhat " up in the air " regarding this bill, especially in view of the opposition now developing from some of my friends in Manitoba who were enthusiastic for it an hour or two ago. They now see the difficulties which some of us older members have seen for years with regard to this particular form of legislation. I pointed out to the minister today, as I have done on several previous occasions, some of the difficulties which we had to deal with in the special committee regarding the character of this legislation. Although the minister has pronounced upon it, I am still of opinion that the arbitration, if any, should be before the county judge only, because I believe that in the great majority of cases, as I have already stated to-day, the matter can be settled as between the officers of the Soldier Settlement Board and the soldier settler himself.
I might go further and say that I am opposed to this bill in toto, for the simple reason that it gives relief to only one class of settlers, and then to a very limited extent -simply to the amount to which that settler is indebted to the government. There can be no justification for legislation of this kind except probably on three grounds: first, as a means of keeping the settler upon the land; second, as relief to the soldier settlers as soldiers, or, third, as a matter of charity. There can be no other grounds for legislation of this kind. If it is the purpose of the bill to keep the soldier settler upon the land, then we should reinstate all those soldiers who have been driven out by action of the Soldier Settlement Board or by adverse circumstances over which they had no control. Nature does not make two men alike-not even officials of the Soldier Settlement Board. At the present time we have officials of this board who are probably rather stringent in dealing with the soldier settler. They have driven hundreds from the land by officious action, by paternal care, and so on. Some of them have even gone to the extent of telling the settlers' wives how to make bread! This is something which can continue only for a limited length of time among free Canadian citizens. As a result some of these men have left the land. Wherever possible they should be reinstated, especially in view of the fact that perhaps the official of the Soldier Settlement Board in the adjoining district has continued men on the land who have made practically no payments for several years. How can you justify driving off his land one man who has made an honest legitimate attempt to continue as a settler, while to another man who has made very little effort, to say the least, you give certain benefits under this measure?
Many of the men who have already left the land have paid a considerable amount of money on account of their holdings and have made certain valuable improvements. I do not need any further proof of this than the statement of the minister himself that the government has made a profit on all the salvaged lands which have been already disposed of. Why was this profit made? Largely because of the initial payments by the soldier settler himself, amounting to at least ten per cent of the purchase money and in many eases much more than that, and also because of the improvements he put on the land. As to this legislation being based on charity, I do not think the government takes that stand. As a matter of fact every argument-

Was it not on
account of crown lands having been sold that the board was ahead of the deal in very many cases after salvaging the soldier settlers' holdings?

I do not think that enters into the case at all. As a matter of fact it only tends to prove my argument. If a man takes unimproved crown land and
Soldier Settlement Act

improves it so that the government makes a profit on its resale, then he should be given consideration for those improvements.

Even if those
lands were not improved, when once the patents were issued to the board would they not be more salable?

A man who took crown
land under the Soldier Settlement scheme received no loan except for improvements or for stock. So he does not come under this bill in any event. As I said before, the third reason which could be ascribed for this bill would be charity, and every argument that has been advanced from this side of the House or elsewhere against the bill will apply equally in that case. Take for example one or two specific instances that I have thought out myself. Take the case of a man who has come over here desiring to be a farmer, and very careful in regard to assuming any financial obligations. He knew his capital was limited, and therefore he purposely purchased a farm with little or no improvements upon it. We will suppose for the sake of argument that he purchased a farm worth $3,000; he paid about $1,000 upon it; he duly made his payments and improved the farm, because naturally in order to keep himself on the land for seven or eight years he would have to improve it. Under this bill that man gets no relief because the farm to-day is worth at least as much as the loan which the government originally advanced upon it. Then take another man, less careful. He buys an adjoining quarter section and pays $5,000 for it, pays 10 per cent down, and to-day is owing the government a large sum of money. Those two farms are now of equal value-the one which was purchased for $5,000 and unimproved since has no greater value than the one which was purchased at $3,000 and upon which the soldier settler has done certain work. In the one case the careful and industrious man will derive no benefit under this bill; in the other case the man of wider ambition, who was less careful and did less work by way of improvement, will receive a large return from the government.
I think I have already told the House that there is another class of settlers, namely, the men who have paid in full; the men who were tired of this paternal care by the Soldier Settlement Board or who perhaps wanted to sell their farms. They went to Tom Jones or Dick Smith or somebody else and borrowed money at 7 per cent or 8 per cent in order to pay for their farms, and that money is still owing. These men are entitled to consideration and I see no reason why any

thoughtful man, desirous of doing the best for the soldiers and the best for Canada, should not be able to give them some relief. If you pass this act as it is you are going to create a dissatisfaction all through the ranks of the men who have gone on these lands, because they will not receive equal treatment.

I have already indicated
definitely my position as to the formation of the tribunal which is to revalue these lands, and I do not intend to repeat what I have already said. If the minister is bent on having an arbitration committee and if that is the prevalent idea in his mind, why not follow-the proper course and give the soldier the right to name his own arbitrator? Did the minister ever hear of an arbitration where more than the presiding arbitrator was named by any outsider? Each side names an arbitrator to act for them; in this case the department would name the arbitrator to act for the board, and the soldier should be allowed to name his arbitrator.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have been trying to meet this difficulty. The wording of that section of the bill is:
-one of whom shall be the judge of the county or district court, as the case may be, of the county or judicial district within which the land is situate, such judge to be the chairman of the committee, one a representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, and one a representative of a veterans' or settlers' organization in the district.
I would be willing to have the third man named by the judge, if that would be satisfactory.

In common with the minister I have only one desire; that is, to get a bill which will be fair to all concerned. Let the bill stand as it is so far as the judge and the nominee of the board are concerned, but let the soldier interested name his own arbitrator. There will then be at least one member of the board whose main duty will be to consider the soldier and get him what he thinks is proper.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to suggest that each individual soldier should name his own man?

Certainly. Does not the minister think that a proposition involving $3,000 or $4,000 or $5,000-every blessed thing the settler has in the world-is of sufficient importance to give him the right to name an arbitrator to act for him in the case? All manner of things are occupying the attention of judges, many of them not amounting to one-tenth or one-twentieth of those sums. I am not varying my views one iota regarding

Soldier Settlement Act
the tribunal, which I think is best for the department and for the soldier, but for some reason or other the minister-I do not think he has given the committee a good reason- seems to be bent on this committee. If that is so, then let him carry out the ideas that have been prevalent in connection with arbitrations of this kind for years and years.
I understood the minister to say that under the provisions of this amended bill soldiers will have the opportunity for a period of six months of returning upon the land and getting the benefit of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
catch my hon. friend's remark.

The minister corrected himself and said October first. The minister did say six months at first, but I will not quibble over that, whether it is October first or six months. In one case it is a three months' period and in the other case six months, but I am not complaining of that. I want to ask the minister if he thinks there is any chance of carrying that out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
follow my hon. friend all the way through.

I will state it again. As I understood him, the minister made the statement that he considered the provisions of this bill open to soldiers for a period of six months, even where the soldier was not upon the land. I now say to the minister that that is not so. In the first place it would be only to October first; it would not be six months, because there is not much chance of this bill becoming law for probably another month. So the soldier would only have about three months left. The section is as follows:
Application for revaluation can be considered only when made by a settler residing on and himself farming the said land-
Then the minister seeks to meet the point raised by referring to October first, which appears in subsection (d) of the same section, as follows:
All applications for revaluation must be submitted to the board prior to the first day of October, 1926.
They must be submitted by men upon the land, and if these men are not upon the land now and this bill does not become law until possibly June first, does the minister seriously think any man is going back upon 9 p.m. the land just in the hope that he may get a revaluation and make something? It was urged upon the minister that the provisions of this act should be open to any soldier not upon the land, but whose land was still unallotted. If the original location is still unoccupied why should not a
soldier make an application, whether or not he is on the land? I believe that is what the minister thought he had done; if he did not think that I do not know why he rose to correct the hon. member who was calling his attention to it. If I am right in assuming that that was his intention I think he will agree that this bill will not produce that result. Is there any reason in the world why a soldier who has vacated land; who has suffered-as we all admit very many of them have suffered-and whose land has not been allotted either under the colonization scheme referred to by the minister or under any other scheme; who has put his good money into it and who is out of pocket, should not be able to make application in connection with that land and get the relief intended by this bill? I urge the minister to consider that feature. It is not going to hurt anyone, because if the land is allotted the soldier is out of it and out of pocket, and the man who has sold his land is out of it also. I know there are difficulties in the way; I know the minister wants to do the best he can, and I think this act should be still further amended in the way I have suggested.

The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) made some reference to the newer members of the House, stating that they were beginning to see light in connection with this question. I may Say that I appreciate very fully the difficulties which confronted the minister in drafting a bill of this kind. I stated so in speaking to the bill when it first came (before this House and I appreciate perhaps a little more to-day the difficulties the minister has had to face in dealing with this situation. I believe the change suggested by the minister will meet the situation, and I cannot agree with the last speaker when he says that each individual soldier should name his own representative. That would be impossible and unreasonable.
Would the hon. member tell me why that would be unreasonable?
Because the expense incurred would make it impossible. It would be too expensive to the settler to have a representative for each separate case coming before the committee.
It would not put the settler to any expense. The representative named by the soldier would be paid by the department, under the provisions of this act.
I differ with you on that point.

I venture to say the minister will not.

Soldier Settlement Act

I cannot speak for the minister, I can only speak for myself. A representative appointed by one of the veterans' organizations, or some similar organization, in the centre of the district in which the soldier settler lives, will be sufficient. I think that one individual on the board could represent the different soldier settlers living in the community. I still stand squarely behind the minister with respect to the committee to be appointed, provided my hon. friend makes the change he suggested just now. That would be the most inexpensive method. It would serve the purpose of the soldier settler better than having him apply to the county court judge to have his grievances remedied.
In the minister's opinion, under the terms of this section, must all three members of the arbitration committee, so-called, agree in order to have a finding? Must they be unanimous in their opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Then if they are not to be unanimous in their opinion, under what provision of the bill is it declared that the opinion of the majority shall prevail? The mere fact of calling this committee an arbitration committee does not imply that the finding of a majority shall prevail. Under the terms of the bill there must be first, a unanimous finding, and I think that point should be carefully considered by the minister.
Furthermore, in subsection (c) there is this provision:
The difference or depreciation in value to be determined .shall be the diminution, not due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, in the present market value of the land as compared with the price at which the settler agreed to purchase the said land from the board-
And then in subsection (h) it is provided:
Upon the hearing of all evidence submitted the committee shall decide the extent to which depreciation in value has taken place and its decision shall be final.
Now, subsection (c) contemplates a finding that no part of the diminution in value is due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of a settler, or if a part of a diminution or depreciation in value is due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler, the settler shall not be allowed such depreciation as is due to neglect or mismanagement, as the case may be. But under subsection (h), when we deal with a finding, all questions as to neglect or mismanagement are excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under
which?

Under sub-section (h), because the committee are to decide, and only to decide, the extent to which depreciation in value has taken place. Now the extent to which depreciation in value has taken place is one thing; the extent to which that depreciation in value is due to mismanagement or neglect on the part of a settler is another, and is not to enter into the decision according to the terms of subsection (h).

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not a lawyer, but is not the direction in sub-section (c) to the arbitration board?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It merely
mentions depreciation.

Sub-section (c) says:
The difference or depreciation in value to be determined shall be the diminution, not due to neglect or mismanagement on the part of the settler-
And so on. I suggest that there is some confusion, because under sub-section (h) you say that the committee shall decide the extent to which depreciation in value has taken place, and its decision shall be final. If that is dealing with the same depreciation that is provided for in sub-section (c), then it is unnecessary. I suggest that a judge of any court would say that there is one provision in sub-section (c) and another in sub-section (h). and that the provision in sub-section (c) wouid necessarily be followed. I suggest in that connection that only a judge who has some knowledge of the law is competent to decide this question of depreciation due to neglect or mismanagement. That is a question that should be left to judicial decision, and I suggest that under this bill it would be far better to leave the matter entirely to the county or district court judge. As the bill now stands I am of the opinion that the committee must be unanimous. If they are not to be unan'.mous, the matter should be decided by the majority, consisting of the judge and one other member. Having got that far, why not leave the decision to the judge after hearing both sides?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does not
my hon. friend see that where three men are appointed there must be provision for decision by a majority? They may decide with the soldier's representative on one occasion, and with the representative of the boaid on another. An agreement by two would constitute a decision, but it would be impossible to have a board of three and have them a."

Soldier Settlement Act
in agreement. Naturally the contestant would want to bring in a minority report, and the thing would be unending.

With great respect to the
minister I suggest that that is exactly what he is providing, whether intentionally or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is certainly not intentional.

I suggest with deference
that under this bill there is clearly no doubt whatever but that committee must be unanimous. There is no provision for a decision of the majority.
I would suggest that the hon. member should look at sub-section (j).

That subsection reads as
follows:
The board may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, make such regulations as may be necessary for the execution of the purposes of this section.
Well, that is as broad as it is possible to make it. But they may only make such regulations as may be necessary, and it is not necessary that two should constitute a quorum of that board. If a fundamental matter requiring the decision of the majority is to be a subject of regulation under sub-sectic.n (j), almost everything conceivable may be provided for. Certainly parliament is not going to give to the minister or to the board, even to the board approved by the Governor in Council, as wide powers as those suggested by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It will be
necessary to give the board fairly wide power. You cannot provide the statute for everything that will crop up. All we want in the statute is the necessary provision for the operation of the board and to give parliament the requisite control.

I appreciate that. All I suggest, with deference, is that a matter so fundamental as to whether the three shall be unanimous, or whether the finding of two shall prevail, cannot be provided for by any regulations passed and approved within the meaning of clause (j). (I do not wish to be too fimciy about the matter, but there are so many "cans", "wills", "mays" and "shalls" in this measure that I do not think anyone in the House could tell exactly what it means.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Better can the bill.

Take clause (h), which reads:
Upon receipt of an application for revaluation supported as aforesaid, the board shall refer the same to the district arbitration committee who will thereupon fix a convenient time and place for hearing.
Certainly the word "will" is not the proper one to carry out what I believe to be the intention of the minister. Then take clause (i), which reads:
The committee shall forthwith forward a copy of its decision to the board, and where the decision shows-
Well, the decision does not show anything.
I do not understand the meaning of the word "show" in that connection. You might say, "where the committee finds or decides". I am convinced that someone in the office of the minister has drafted these amendments hurriedly, and without due care to provide that the diction shall be so clear as to obviate litigation.
Mr. CAHiLI: I desire to make a suggestion to the minister, as this appears to be the time for makiug suggestions and several have been made by members of the opposition. My underst inding of the bill is that it is a measure designed to get a lot of people out of trouble which they have got into on account of the action of the Tory party in the past. It was designed and drafted by the Liberal government in an attempt to relieve thousands of soldiers in the country of obligations that they undertook at the instigation of the Tory party in previous years. It was presented to the House, and in less than an hour I have heard at least five suggestions from members of the opposition in regard to various ways of constituting this board.-The suggestion is made by the leader of the opposition that it should be left to the county court judge, then the Conservative whip (Mr. Boys) sitting immediately behind the right hon. leader, suggests that it should be determined by a board of three.
No. If the hon. member had been attending to his duties in the House this afternoon he would have heard the very reverse.
Did my hon. friend not suggest a moment ago, as to the method of appointing the tribunal, that one should be appointed by the soldier himself?

If the hon. gentleman had listened he would have heard me declare my views as to what the tribunal should consist of, namely, the county court judge. But I said that if the minister insisted on the
Soldier Settlement Act

arbitration idea, involving a board of three, the soldier should have the right to name one arbitrator.

That is it exactly-that the soldier should have the right to appoint one of the arbitrators if there were to be three. Another hon. member a few moments ago suggested five, and he was kind enough to allow the government to appoint one of the five, provided the minister now in charge of the bill should be in charge of the matter during the administration of the measure. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not endorse the suggestion of my right hon. friend, and apparently there is no agreement among hon. members on the other side. They got these men into the mess and now they are not willing to let the government get them out of it. The government prepared the bill; why not let them take the responsibility of doing the best they can for these men? The whole difficulty seems to be that members of the opposition think some person is going to get a little political kudos out of it. After the discussion this afternoon in regard to this measure, if these soldiers are not turned against the opposition I do not think anything they can do in the future could have that effect. After listening to the suggestions of the opposition on a bill promoted by the government for the purpose of getting these men out of a difficulty in which they have been placed by the opposition, I suggest to the minister he should ask the committee to rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, until my hon. friends have had time to consult with the people vitally interested, the soldiers, and ascertain what they have .to say about it. I am quite satisfied the soldiers will tell hon. members opposite that they had better let the government go ahead with the business and not do any more blockading, such as they have been doing for the last few days.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend
from Pontiac will forgive me if I do not refer to his speech, but say a few words on the bill. The main purpose of any bill is to express the will of the House as to what should be done to meet the purpose of such bill, whatever it may be.
The will of the majority of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If we are all ready to let the minister do what he likes, it can be done very simply. I ask the minister if he would support the bill if it read this way:
The minister may appoint district arbitration committees having jurisdiction in such soldier settlement 
districts as may be necessary, each committee to consist of three members, one of whom shall be the judge of the county or district court, as the case maybe, of the county or judicial district within which the land is situate, such judge to be the chairman of the committee, and the others the president and secretary of the Liberal Association, or whoever else the minister likes.
Would the minister support the clause if it read that way, and appoint either the
president or secretary of the Liberal Association or whomever he likes? The clause as it reads has precisely the same effect; under it the minister can appoint whomever he likes as the other two arbitrators; he can appoint the president and secretary of the Liberal Association or anybody he desires to appoint. It is-true the bill says that one shall be the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, but he does not need to be an officer of the board in order to be a representative. He can appoint a Chinaman if he likes and call him. the representative of the board, or he can appoint a Japanese, and call him the representative of a soldiers' organization. He does not need to be an officer of the board. But hon. members say the minister will not do that. Well, why are we inserting this clause in the bill? Why not let the minister do as he likes? Word the bill in this way:
That as respects what the soldier shall pay on any land he gets, the Minister of the Interior may, in the exercise of his mature judgment, and in the light of his Scriptural teaching, do whatever he pleases.
We might as well pass such legislation as that. The duty of the House is so to word the bill as to guard the public interest as best we can. That is the purpose of the wording. I. repeat: The word "representative" does not. mean, as hon. members seem to assume, that a man to be a representative of soldiers' organization is selected by them or is even a member of the organization. He does not need to-be that. The minister can go into Marquette, select the president of the Liberal association and say to him: You are on the arbitration board for Marquette district and you represent the soldiers' organization. It may be said that he cannot do so. Very well, what is the legislation for? He can appoint somebody else and say: You are the representative for the Soldier Settlement Board-and that man does not need to be an officer of the board at all. Surely the minister would not pass the legislation if it was worded as I read it first, but the way he has it in this bill it has exactly the same effect: his powers are just as ample; the meaning is just the same. Surely that is not good legislating.
I know we are taking some time, but the minister is on the wrong line, to begin with; and in the next place the legislation is sloppy.

Soldier Settlement Act
It is crude in its whole verbiage; it is not carefully conceived. I have given the minister credit for having in mind only a good bill, a method of working this thing out aright; but he has had no excuse at all for tying to the tail of a judge any two arbitrators of any kind. What does the minister want them for? He is opening the door to fraud. He may not mean to do that and I know he does not mean to; but why do it? It does not matter what he means; if the door is open he can take it for granted that frauds will be committed. He has opened the door to anyone who may be in charge, who desires to act fraudulently in a district, to do so. The door will be just as wide open as anything in the world ever was.
The suggestions have been simple; there has been nothing complex about them. The suggestions are simply these: Follow the same course that you follow in expropriations, that you follow in assessments, that you follow in relation to any other matter' where the crown and the individual under the crown are concerned; simply have the judge hear the evidence and decide. If the minister then cares to provide-and I think he probably would-some means of enabling the soldier to conduct his case, that is a simple matter. Discretion should be given to the judge in that regard to give the soldier a certain allowance up to a limit say, under such conditions that might be framed by regulation. That is only a detail, but the essence of the whole thing is to get your tribunal sound and to get the principle sound upon which the tribunal acts. If the minister gets that done, the rest is not of as great consequence although it is of consequence, of course. If you are bound to move on this line, putting it on a basis of helping rather than on a basis of protection, then you are certainly going to have to extend it to those men who are off the land, whether they were put off or not, and you have to get it just as was indicated in the speech of the hon. member just behind. These are the two main factors if the minister would consider them. It is not that we are wanting to complain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend is speaking only for himself in that respect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know there are one or two misconceptions of the effect of the bill, but I am not speaking only for myself or only for this side of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is again misquoting me, for this reason:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am saying that the
minister has not his bill wide enough in the personnel; he did not have it wide enough in the beginning. He is having it apply to a class of cases it does not need to apply to, but there are more cases on the other side to which it does not apply and he is going to have it applied to them. If he does not do so this year, he will next year; he cannot get out of doing it. What I am driving at now -and it is really the main feature-is that he should get his principle right as to the tribunal. That is the simplest thing in the world. The clause could be worded in two minutes; we would then be past that, and I venture to say that we would be past it with the overwhelming concurrence of this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The appointment of a judge alone?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I doubt it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister does not do this, the complications he is going to get into will certainly foe very great. Does he imagine he is going to satisfy soldiers' organizations by naming a mam? speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The leader of the opposition is quite correct when he suggests that if the president and secretary of the Liberal association were named, I would object to the bill. Any sensible man would.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister interrupted me several times and I was glad to have those interruptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, when my right hon. friend strays too far from the path of rectitude. It is useless to argue that such a construction as my right hon. friend has just indicated could be placed upon the wording of the bill. That is the furthest thing from the intention of the bill. If I have told the House once, I have told it fifty times that I have no desire to name these men. I did not think I was naming them. My right hon. friend put that construction on the bill. I do not think he understood the intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is not the ordinary case that we are dealing with, nor have we ever dealt with soldiers' problems from the standpoint of sending them to the courts as the courts exist to-day. On every occasion we have appointed a committee of this House, accepted the finding of that committee and put it into effect. It can be said that committees of this House have been too generous in the past. I had no thought on earth of dictating to the board as to the appointment of their representatives. The only reason the word "representative" is in this bill is that we did not want to name definitely the field or district supervisor, because in some cases these men might not be the proper persons to act for the board. That is all; otherwise we would have named the district supervisor as the individual to be upon that committee. Apparently there is a desire to nail this thing down- to a hard and fast rule. It is not the case -that the government or the minister wants to have jurisdiction in the matter or to -make it a political machine as some hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think. Our anticipation is that this bill will do the government far more harm with the returned soldier than it will do it good. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to take the responsibility of it, I shall be glad to give it -to them, because I think the government that handles this matter will lose -more votes than it will gain. -That is my candid opinion.

Mr. MEI-QHEN: We are trying to help it so that it will not hurt you.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I question that. However, the government must assume the responsibility. It does not rest upon my hon. friends opposite but upon us, and if wre take that responsibility we must have something to say about the bill. I am not criticizing the suggestions that have been offered and I certainly do not think anyone can charge me with having done so. I have sat here and tried to gather from the various suggestions that have been put forward some idea of what kind of measure would best meet the view of the House as a whole. When the bill is passed -it is scarcely likely to satisfy everyone. With due respect to the legal fraternity as represented in this House, I venture to say that no bill that might be enacted here would meet with their entire approval: there would be some who would have some fault to find with it. At any rate I have not yet seen one measure pass that was agreed to unanimously, and I have seen a good many go through all the stages of legislation in this House.
M-r. BOYS: Is it the intention that a majority of the members of the tribunal shall have the right to give a decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
-Certainly.
My hon. -friend does not think that it would be necessary to have an entire agreement, for in that case there would be no decision.
No, but there should be some provision whereby any two of the three might bring in an award.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are a number of things in this bill which will have to be left to regulation.

The decision is the decision of the board as an entity and it must therefore be the decision of the whole three, unless you provide in the bill that the voice of two shall speak for the board as a whole.

As regards the possibility of appointments being made from political considerations, I would bring to the minister's attention what occurred in connection with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, under the Hon. Mr. Beland. That was much more a soldier organization than is the Soldier Settlement Board, for, as the hon. member (Mr. Power) pointed out this afternoon, the Soldier Settlement Board' was originally established as a settlement scheme. The Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, on the contrary, was essentially an organization to serve the interests of the soldiers themselves, and not-

Soldier Settlement Act
withstanding that fact changes were made in the medical personnel throughout the country for no other than political reasons. Many such changes were made. If, therefore, there was that danger in connection with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, because the medical officers who were displaced were of the wrong political colour, is there not the same danger, indeed, a greater danger, in this case where the organization is not so peculiarly one in the interests of the soldiers?
I do not charge the minister with anything of that kind-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You cannot, because I have made no changes in the board.
I have no doubt that the minister is sincere in his desire to put through a proper measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will not argue that the officers of the board were appointed because they were Liberals.

What I am saying is that changes were made in the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment because of political considerations, Conservatives being replaced by Liberals. And this occurred not in one instance, but in many. At the head of the lakes a Conservative who had served in the lines overseas was replaced by a Liberal who had never been out of Canada, and the same is true of the constituency represented by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Ross). I have heard that hon. member make a similar statement regarding certain officers in his section of the country. The fact of the matter is that throughout Canada changes were made in the personnel of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment because the incumbents who were ousted happened to be of the. wrong political persuasion. Now that, as I haive said, was essentially a soldier organization, whereas the board we are discussing was established primarily as a means of settling soldiers. I argue, therefore, that there is a greater danger of political influence being brought to bear in this matter than in the other. I give the minister credit for sincerity and I think he should be only too willing to avoid the possibility of having this legislation used as a political machine. He can help to this end by allowing the judge to be the sole arbitrator in these cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: The committee is dealing with the Minister of Interior at present; it can deal with the Minister of Agriculture when agricultural matters are under consideration. I make that perfectly plain to the committee, because the government must take responsibility for the bill. Further, I am prepared to amend the clause relating to the classes to be dealt with.

If the minister accepts the suggestion of the hon. member with regard to the representative of the soldier, I would suggest, in order to preclude such an interpretation as was indicated by the leader of the opposition, that it be made to read "an appointee of the Soldier Settlement Board " instead of a representative.

speechtext:
He will be
an appointee of the board, but the minister will reserve the right to make that particular appointment. The government must have some representation, but there will be no interference on the part of the minister. I am prepared to widen the scope of the bill to deal with every man whose contract is not cancelled, but I will not go further, because to do so to an unlimited degree would only create untold complications.
