The minister referred to "any man whose contract is not cancelled." Will that include those men whose contracts are closed by payment in full?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all; they are in the same position as those who have cancelled their contracts.
The contracts are determined.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. It
covers only the man whose contract is in existence and who owes the government a substantial sum of money on it.

I would point out to the
minister that if he does insert-and he certainly must insert as a fundamental provision of this bill-that the decision of the majority shall prevail, he cannot do so under this clause.
Mr. STEW'ART (Edmonton):	I propose
to amend it.

Then I would call attention to this objection. Provision being made that if the arbitration committee, so-called, is not necessarily unanimous the finding of two of the arbitrators will prevail, it is quite possible for two members other than the judge to unite to oust the judge entirely. Thereupon you have two members of the committee rendering a majority decision opposed to that of the judge on whatever legal questions may arise. I suggest to the minister that he make his amendment read so that one member of the majority of two must be the judge, otherwise it is utterly useless to have a judge as one of the members of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) apparently is not very sure as to what the bill really means. After listening to all the discussion that has taken place, I have not been able to apprehend the meaning of the suggestions that have been made other' than that the county court judge shall decide all the circumstances. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) seemingly is very much afraid that the tribunal will in reality be a political machine. I do not think there is much danger of that if the right people are chosen.
Oh, oh.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I have not lost faith in human nature yet. Polities is bad enough, but I believe men can be found to act honestly and uprightly, no matter whether they be Conservatives or Liberals. As I mentioned before, I have had some experience as a member of a tribunal ascertaining the value of land. Land valuation is a very difficult and complicated problem. No man can tell what is the value of a certain portion of land. The only criterion of its value is what anyone is willing to pay for it. That, is the only real basis of valuation.

No, no.

Soldier Settlement Act

Some of my hon. friends
say, "No, no;" but there is no oth^f way of ascertaining the value of land except on the basis of what somebody will pay to get hold of it. The value goes up and down and a great many things enter into the question. Now, a judge may be the very best qualified individual to decide certain legal questions, but I doubt if he is best fitted to give a final decision on the value of land. He is learned in many ways, he is perhaps a good judge of human nature, which, of course, is of great assistance to him in weighing evidence, but, that evidence must be adduced by people who know what they are talking about. Consequently if he has the other two members of that board sitting with him, and they have a pretty good idea of the value of land, I think perhaps he can perform a very useful function in weighing the evidence adduced. In regard to who two of the arbitrators should be, I think the minister would be well advised to take a man representing the soldier settlers in the district. It should not be at all difficult in any particular locality to divide it into districts, and then let the soldiers in those several districts elect someone to be their representative upon the board. I am sure those soldier settlers are so earnest in their desire to get a thoroughly competent board that they would not worry whether their representative was a Conservative, a Progressive or a Liberal. Undoubtedly they would select the best man available to represent them. Although technically the minister is head of the Soldier Settlement Board, I do not think that even members of the opposition believe he is going to interfere with the arbitrator that will be chosen to represent the Soldier Settlement Board. It does seem to me that those two arbitrators with the county court judge ought to constitute a board that will be just as near satisfactory as you can get it. I am quite aware that no matter how you set about doing it, this work will be beset with difficulties and will not give satisfaction to a number of soldier settlers; but we have simply to do the very best we can under the circumstances. I do believe that most hon. members are really anxious to get something that will be as nearly satisfactory as possible. I think I would agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that the judge should form one of the majority of the committee when the decision is not unanimous. There is something in the argument of the leader of the opposition that there might be some collusion between the soldier settler representative and the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board, and consequently 14011-153J
the common interest might not be taken care of just as carefully as it should be. By making the judge one of the majority I think we shall guard against that contingency.
The minister is altogether too apologetic. I think he ought to make up his mind just exactly what he wants, and fight for it. However, I am inclined to believe the criticisms have been offered in good faith and that we are all anxious to do the best we can for the soldier settler. I have been getting letters every day, in fact I got two to-day, voicing objection to a judge being the final arbitrator. I can understand how the soldier settlers may take that point of view, and of course there are two sides to every question. I have a long letter and quite a large petition from British Columbia-I think they are from the group of men referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)-and all those people are against the judge having the sole authority. This is a serious question which is going to cost a good deal of money, and I am inclined to agree with the minister that the government will not come through with very much glory when they finish. I am perfectly sure of that.

Would the hon. member
tell us from whom he received the petition, and its contents?

I could not do that because I have not the petition with me, but it is no secret; I will let the hon. member see it if he so desires. I think I have received more complaints in regard to this question from British Columbia than from any other province; I believe I receive more letters touching this matter than do most of the members of my group, and I find a great deal of dissatisfaction in British Columbia and in Manitoba. I do not know that I have added anything to the value of this debate, but I hope we can get together and work out something which will be satisfactory to everyone.
Would the hon. member allow a question?
Yes.

In a three-man board does
not the county court judge become the final arbiter?
Not necessarily so.

Why not, if there is any
dispute?

The other two members of
the board1 might agree and would form a majority, leaving the judge in the minority.
Soldier Settlement Act

Then there would be no
dispute between the other two parties.

What I suggested was that
the majority would have to ibe composed of one of the other members and the judge.
Is not the judge always the final arbiter, if he constitutes the majority?

Supposing the other
two members decide 'against the judge; he would not have anything to say about it at all.

I suppose that difficulty
might 'arise. However, I have said all that I propose to say in regard to the matter. I am quite satisfied that we will never get a bill with which everyone will be satisfied, but we are going to do the best we can. I have had a little experience with appeals to a judge, and I can tell hon. members that this is going to be very unpopular with the county court judges. They do not want this work, and do not like it. I know that the judges are honourable and patriotic and will undertake the duty, but they will not like the work.

I just wanted to ask
the hon. member a question before he closes and I am quite conscious of the
10 p.m. fact that he is just as anxious as anyone to find a real solution to this question. Would he object to the department being represented by one man, the soldier represented by one man, these two appearing before the judge and the judge giving a decision after considering all the facts?

I think what I have already said would almost lead to that conclusion. There is not very much difference of opinion in regard to the advisability of having those two representatives; the only difference which exists at present is as to the standing they should have. The recommendation of the right hon. leader of the opposition I believe, was that the judge should sit as a judge, with the others appearing as witnesses. Under the other plan, instead of appearing only as witnesses they would be members of the board and would have more standing in that way.
I would like to refer for just a moment to the question of expense. We are not going to add much to the expense by enlarging the board to three. It may be rather arbitrary to put any such regulation into the act, but I would almost be prepared to say

that no lawyer should appear before that board. I am quite well aware that we cannot do without the lawyers in a great many cases; we have found that out by experience, but this is one of the cases where we can get along without their help. I was chairman of a court which held sessions all over the province of Manitoba, and in every place where lawyers appeared we were held up. If we undertook to value land and inquire as to the assessment we generally could get somewhere, but if lawyers appeared in the case it took us hours to get anywhere. 1 hope the legal members of the House will pardon my references.

In the way this debate has
swung around-I might say rambled around -on the several phases of this bill we have a good illustration of the troubles we get into in departing from the well established rules of the House, sanctioned by years of experience. It has been well known that in a committee we can only debate one section of a bill at a time. Had we not departed from that custom to-day and the last time this bill was being discussed we would have made more progress. As the debate has gone on, one man has spoken of the first section, and following him someone else speaks about the last section. If we had only started at one end of the bill we would have made some progress, and I hope that rule will be adhered to in the future.
I would like to support a portion of the remarks of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys). He brought forward a case which has been brought up again and again during the last two or three days, the case of men who have been what is popularly known as salvaged-that is the technical term -or who have been thrown off or have abandoned their farms. They are off the land. A number of hon. members have made representations on behalf of those men, urging that they be given at least an opportunity to go back on the land again at the reduced value, if such be granted by the board. The minister said twice to-day that he was prepared to make an arrangement of that character; where the land had not been disposed of to an empire settler or in any other way, he was prepared to give the soldier a chance to go back. I do not believe many would return, for many reasons. Most of them are sick of it, but I think it would be the proper thing to give them a chance. I was going to rise when I heard him make that remark early this afternoon and again this evening; I wanted to ask that that be put

Soldier Settlement Act
into the bill, because we all know that utterances made on the floor of this House are not bound up in the bill and form no portion of it. Withii^ the last few minutes, however, the minister stated, if I have not misunderstood him-and if I have I hope he will correct me-that he would not give any instructions to include the man whj has had his agreement cancelled. I think it was agreed by the House that these men should get some consideration, and I think the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Hannesson) was also going to raise that point. I would like ro ask the minister to make that promise agam, and to allow it to be put into the bill in order that these men may have an opportunity of going back again.

The minister made a statement a moment ago that he would not look after anyone who had left the land. I want to remind him that the last time this matter came up he gave an undertaking that the desired provision in that respect would be embodied in the bill. Now I want to ask him this question: Is he or is he not willing to extend the scope of the bill to cover the revaluation of all salvaged lands undisposed of by the board, so that any former settler may make application and be entitled to the benefit if he can establish to the satisfaction of the board that he has proper qualifications and is financially able to carry on without further assistance? I gave the minister a copy of the memorandum I have here, so that this question will not surprise him. I only ask that the privilege be extended for a matter of two months in respect of a man v'hose land is still in the hands of the board, and for four months in the matter of the selection of any other lands the board still hold.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
follow my hon. friend. He suggests that the soldier settler be allowed a period of two months.
That he be given a preference for two months.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We certainly made a promise that we would give consideration to those cases where salvaging was going through, or in cases where we had not allocated the land.
Not disposed of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Or disposed of it by allotment or in some other way. I want to make it perfectly clear we are not considering the case of the man whose lands
have been salvaged and are gone, but in cases where salvaging has just gone through, the hope was entertained that we might be able to get those men back. There are a thousand and one difficulties in the way of dealing with a man who is off his land and gone. He still owes the government in many eases a considerable amount of money, his stock and implements have been sold. This illustrates the difficulties that arise. But in the case of the man who can re-establish himself and has not been allocated his land we are prepared not only to receive his application but to notify him that if he wants to come back we will give him reasonable time to re-establish himself.

Will the time be
extended?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This man simply comes back and gets into the same position as the man who has not left his land at all.

I understand the minister is prepared in the case of the empire settlement scheme to give settlers there the land on the revaluation basis. I am not asking anything in respect of land that was abandoned, but in respect of any soldier settler lands we give the returned man who is qualified and does not need further financial assistance the opportunity to buy at the revaluation figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
right.

In making a resale to a soldier settler is the minister prepared to give credit for the amount of principal paid by the settler in the past on the revaluation figure? That point is also mentioned in the memorandum I give him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as his payments were concerned he would have to go back just as he stood.
He would receive no credit for past principal payments?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would be in exactly the same position as if he had not left the land; he would be in no better or no worse position.
Suppose he goes on another piece of land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That would raise complications. It is a most difficult thing to settle. The man will be beginning
Soldier Settlement Act

all over again. I am not prepared to give my hon. friend a direct answer; I want time to consider that.

I understand the minister's
answer to the last question is that in that case the soldier and his agreement will be reinstated, and he will get the benefit of the reduction on revaluation as though he had not been put off the land at all and his original agreement had not been determined.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
conceive of any other condition.

That is the position I understand the minister to take. I understand he is also prepared to amend the bill so as to embody this provision in the measure and not leave it to be provided for by regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid we cannot do that without making many amendments in the old act. What is proposed is a very simple process. We will treat cases of the kind as though salvage had not taken place.

Surely the minister could put
something in the bill providing that in cases where an agreement has been determined, or is in process of determination through the *board, on the fulfilment of certain conditions the agreement that has been or is being determined on that ground may be reinstated, and the man may come under the provisions of the bill in the same way as though he had not [DOT]forfeited his rights. The trouble is just this: I can see that the important provisions of the bill are apparently going to be in the regulations and that is a very pernicious practice. [DOT]We do not want the provisison of the bill to be in the regulations, and leave these regulations at the mercy and under the control of *an order in council. The House ought to *pass on all the important substantive provisions of the bill.
There is one further observation I should like to make in this connection. I cannot see how the country can suffer by allowing a soldier settler who has forfeited his agreement and been put off his land coming forward as a new man, making an application, and getting a preference for the purchase of other lands that are still in the hands of the government. All those lands will have to be put up for sale and they can only be sold to [DOT]proper and competent purchasers at a fair value at the time the sale is made. Now, if the soldier who had forfeited his agreement because of the excessive price that he paid *for his land is now in a position to become a *purchaser of other lands at the price at which 
the government would sell them to a stranger, why should he not have the right to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no particular objection, but should the payments he had made on the former land be carried forward?

I did not quite catch the minister's question, but my contention is this: I cannot see what objection there is to allowing a returned soldier who has not had his agreement determined, from purchasing land on the same conditions as an ordinary settler.
There is one other matter I should like to mention, and that involves going back for a minute to the question of the personnel of the arbitration board. If the minister is determined to have his board of three, may I again urge in support of the position taken by the hon. member (Mr. Boys) the suggestion which the minister said he was prepared to adopt, namely, that the soldier himself have the right to make the appointment of his representative. It has been stated that the better way would be to allow the soldiers in a certain district, either through their constituted organizations or any new organization, to appoint a representative in their behalf. Now the difficulty is that where a soldier has confidence in the soldier organization of his district he will in any event probably accept the appointee of that organization, but it is not at all uncommon for an individual soldier not to be in particular favour or in good standing with the soldier organization of his district. If he is in sympathy with and has confidence in the soldier organization of his district, he will accept their nominee anyway; even if you leave to him the power of appointing his own nominee he will probably appoint the nominee chosen by them, whereas if you get the occasional man, as you are bound to do, who has not the sympathy or the support of the soldiers' organization, he may desire to appoint his own nominee. I would suggest, therefore, that the soldier would in all cases be in a better position if he were to appoint his own nominee on tile board. It is not an unusual proceeding. In every arbitration where there is a dispute between two parties each party appoints his own arbitrator, and the third arbitrator is selected by the two arbitrators. There is no reason why, in a dispute between an individual soldier and the Soldier Settlement Board, the same thing should not be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
propose to change the arbitration board in any particular, except to accept the suggestion

Soldier Settlement Act
made by my hon. friend (Mr. Boys), namely, that the soldier shall appoint his own arbitrator. The other two shall remain as they are, the judge and the representative of the Soldier Settlement Board.

I desire to express my appreciation of the consideration given by the minister to my suggestion, but I observe that he seems to rather reluctantly accept the suggestion regarding the right of the soldier to name his own arbitrator. I should not think the minister would accept it if he did not think it was practicable. I believe it is practicable, and I suggest to him that in providing for that he should insert a clause making it necessary that the arbitrator to act for the soldier shall be a landowner resident in the judicial district in which the land is situate. That would avoid any chance of the soldier appointing a man residing many miles away. Where one such soldier has been acting, assuming he is a capable man, the chances are that other soldiers coming before the same judge and the same arbitrator appointed by the board will accept that nominee as his nominee as well, and in that way I do not think there would be very much embarrassment in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member not think it would complicate the matter if we inserted these provisions? It would be much simpler to let the soldier nominate his own representative; then one man may be chosen for two or three dozen. But if you start in by saying that he must be a farmer-
I said a resident.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I prefer to
leave it open; let him have a free choice and not tie him up in any way.

I am quite satisfied Remarks have been made of a critical nature. -I understood we were making these suggestions at the request of the minister, and I offer no apology for any time I have taken up. This is a matter involving millions of dollars, and even if the discussion has taken all the afternoon and part of this evening, the time has been well spent. The minister must feel that some improvement has been made on the previous legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the committee agree I should like to run over the bill, because when I bring it back I desire to have it in such form that it wiil meet die suggestions, as far as practicable, that would appear to be acceptable; then, we would not have to
spend a great deal of time upon it. I take it there is no objection to clause I of 68. I propose to amend sub-section (a) by striking out all the words after "revaluation" down to the word "and" in the third line, so that it will read:
Application for revaluation shall be submitted to the district superintendent of the Soldier Settlement Board for the district within which the said land is situate.
That strikes out the provision that he shall be on the land, and it takes in all the soldiers whose contracts are in existence.
Read clause 68, section (1). just before that. There is a limitation still in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In answer
to what the hon. member for East Edmonton has said, I am informed by the chairman of the board that they have authority now to rescind cancellation proceedings and reinstate the former owner of the land, provided, of course, that they have not disposed of the land; and as a matter of fact they are doing it. So that provision is made for that case. Without amending the act the board has that authority.

I know that, but they could
not exercise that authority unless you strike out these words, because these words shall surely conclude them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If they
reinstated them now they would not have authority to reduce the value of the property.

So far as
the arbitration board is concerned, the matter has been amply discussed and the minister tells us what he intends to do. But I am still concerned with the question of the man who is on the land. There is the further point of the settler who definitely left the land. That is what we are considering here. I want to cite a case where the soldier, having come to the conclusion that the land was too highly valued, left it and definitely abandoned it. The minister has stated that he would be prepared to consider allowing a man to go back on the land if his agreement had not been cancelled. There is some indefiniteness as to what that means, because I do not think the board takes any formal cancellation proceedings. If the man walks off, they have the authority to salvage the farm and realize on it? Assuming a man has to all intents and purposes left the farm; you now decide to revalue that farm. I want that man to have the right to go back to the board and say. "On your revaluation I want to go back on that land". I think that point is under con-
Soldier Settlement Act

sideration. I gathered1, when this matter was being discussed the other day, and recently to-night, that in the view of the minister, if such a man would satisfy the board he was a good risk and was not going to ask for any further commitment from the board by way of advance of moneys, the matter of taking him back on the land would be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the land had not been disposed of.

Yes. I think the House is generally agreed that he should be permitted to go back on the land. Then I think we must amend the bill to make it read in this way. If the minister were dealing with it, I have no doubt he would let the man go back; but in the administration of this measure, whether it be by a board of arbitration or by a judge, you will find that when a man comes to that board asserting a right, they will go to the legislation and say: We have no discretion. Anyone who has had experience with pensions knows that the Board of Pension Commissioners, however philanthropic may be their intention, go to the act and say: We have no discretion. The same thing will ultimately apply to this measure of relief. The arbitration board or the judge will turn to this amendment and will say: Those are our powers. I suggest to the minister that in order to carry out this intention he should so amend the bill as to say in. effect that not only those who are residing on the land, as section 68 (1) says, but soldier settlers who, having left their farms, now desire to go back to farms which have not been allotted on the revaluation scheme, shall be entitled to apply for revaluation.

In that connection I should like to ask the minister if such a returned soldier will have the benefit of and be given credit for his former payments on that land, that is in case a soldier is allowed to go back on land that he previously left, the contract perhaps having been cancelled. In some cases he may have paid a sum of money almost as much as the land is revalued at. Is the minister prepared to say whether in such a case the soldier would be given credit for the amount of money he had previously paid, or must he start at the bottom again and pay for the land practically twice over?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I thought I made it clear to the committee twice this evening that the soldier would be re-established in the same position he was in when he left the land, and that whatever principal

payments had been credited to him would still be to his credit. He might have paid a great deal of interest, but that does not apply on principal payments on the land. He would be in the same position as the man who had stayed on the land and made his payments, when we can replace him on his own land. A suggestion has been made from the opposition that not only should we dn that, but we should allow men to go back and take other land. In that case he could not be given credit for any payments.
Does the minister say that interest payments on the higher valuation will be charged against the soldier's account?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You would get into a hopeless tangle if you started to take interest payments into consideration. Whatever principal payments a man has made against his property would naturally apply, but his interest payments are simply interest payments he has made on the land at the valuation whether high or low.
Will the minister answer the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) about amending the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I would say that this is not the regular routine mortgage foreclosure proceeding. The board have authority under the act to cancel the agreement with the settler and he is simply served with a notice. What they do is simply to rescind that cancellation when the land is available and not to wait for him to make application, but at once to offer it to him if he wants to come back, provided- and there will always have to be a proviso

that he is morally and otherwise a fit man to come back. There are a great many cases in which it would be a mistake to try to make a man come back; to make it indiscriminate that he should be allowed to come back without let or hindrance is out of the question. But in a case where he wants to come back and he can re-establish himself on the land, that course would be adopted. We have that authority in the act at the moment.
It does not seem to be so to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, they are doing it, although they may be doing it contrary to the act. Of course they cannot reduce the value. The amendments will take care of that situation.

Soldier Settlement Act

In the event of the suggestion that came principally from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Hannesson) being adopted, what would happen in the case of a salvaged soldier whose chattels were all gone? It would be impossible for such a man to re-establish himself in order to come under this legislation. I am not sure that that point has been made clear. I have remarked that members making these suggestions, I think without exception, are members who are not soldiers or not farmers.

The hon.
gentleman is making a mistake.

If hon. members understood the matter as we understand it who have gone through t'he school of experience, they would know that not one per cent of those who have already been salvaged will even make application. I am certain that is the case in my riding. I think we are spending a great deal of time over something that will never happen. We are endeavouring to develop an impossible case. I should like to see, if this suggestion is adopted, that that, soldier is put back in the same position he occupied before he was salvaged; otherwise, he is still tremendously discriminated against. I wonder if the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has thought out that phase of the question.

If the suggestion made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) is followed it will mean great expense to the country. The committee cannot meet to consider every individual application for a revaluation. Supposing the committee announce that they will sit at a certain place to hear applications for revaluation. If such individual sdldier has the right to name his own representative on the committee and if you have fifty cases coming before the committee, you will have fifty soldiers' representatives present, and according to the bill we shall have to appropriate money to pay those representatives. That is my understanding of the bill, and therefore I say that the suggestion of the hon. member for North Simcoe is in my opinion impracticable and would prove costly to the country. If we had committees in one or two hundred different districts of the Dominion sitting at the same time and had an army of a thousand individuals representing the soldier settlers, that would mean a large expense to the country. It seems to me that the scheme is unworkable. I would suggest that the veterans' organizations in the different districts nominate the man who is to represent the soldiers. That, I think, would be more satisfactory to the returned men; it would be more workable, and it would be less expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I want to amend the bill now so that at least we may get something fairly satisfactory, because I can assure the committee that I shall not attempt to change it further. If it is objected to on the next introduction I will withdraw it. And that is no idle threat, because it is an absolute impossibility to secure a measure that will meet the views of the committee as a whole if there is to be no give and take. If on the other hand the government takes full responsibility for the bill I will put it through, but I will not spend an inordinate length of time over it. We have been discussing it now almost three days, and while I do not suggest for a moment that the time has been wasted, I do say that the committee should allow it to go through. Having tried as far as I possibly can to meet the general wish of the committee, I trust that the bill will now be allowed to go through. As regards (a) we shall now include all contracts that are in good standing as well as those that are being rescinded where the land has not been allocated. We are already able, however, to deal with such cases.

The minister might add a
provision in respect of agreements which are reinstated by the board under the existing act and in respect of which the land has not been allocated. I understand that he is going to amend the bill in relation to agreements that are in process of rescission.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is to
say, where the land has not been allocated but is still in the hands of the board. As I have pointed out, we have authority already to deal with such cases.
That is all I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be no necessity for adding an amendment to that effect because the board is already empowered in that respect, although it has not the authority to revalue. That authority is being given by this legislation. The board at present can put the soldier back on the land while it is in their hands.

That is all I am suggesting, to bring within the purview of the bill the agreements that are reinstated by the board under its existing powers.
Soldier Settlement Act

I think it will be necessary
to amend line 13 to conform with line 20 in paragraph (a).

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As amended, paragraph (a) will read:
Application for revaluation shall foe submitted to the district superintendent of the Soldier Settlement Board for the district within which the said land is situate.

With the words struck out by that amendment the paragraph provides that the application for revaluation may be considered only when made by a settler residing on and himself farming the land. If a man is not residing on the land I should think that he has abandoned it. So that if you omit these words in paragraph (a) and do not strike out in line 13 the words "who has not abandoned his land" the two paragraphs will conflict.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that line 13 refers to the case in which there is a quit claim.

If that is the meaning of the paragraph I think the language is unfortunate. I do not want to be critical but I do not think you can say that a man has not abandoned his land merely because he has not given you a quit claim deed. When he leaves the land he abandons it whether he gives such a deed or not. I do not want the minister to make the amendment now. I simply bring the matter to his attention because I think it would be wise to make that change.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to a man who is temporarily off the land?

Subsection (1) reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the board is hereby empowered upon the application of a settler who has agreed to purchase any land from the board, who has not abandoned his land-
And so forth. The last clause in that paragraph, as I have quoted it, means that the man must be still on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has not abandoned the land if his contract is not cancelled. If he has abandoned the land then he is outside the provisions of the act.

You should provide for all
cases where the contract has not been cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
covered that.

There is a distinction
between abandonment and temporary absence.

I do not want to worry the
minister; indeed, I want to compliment him on the extraordinary patience he has shown in this matter, and I am convinced that he is most sincere in his desire to do what is best. I will therefore say no more but simply bring the point to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
follow the argument of my hon. friend, and I want to understand it, because I do not wish to bring the bill back again unless I have it as nearly as possible in final shape.
I understand the minister does not expect to do it at this moment. I propose that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. The
committee will not rise until I get a definite idea of where we are going to land with this bill, because, as I say, when I bring it back I do not propose to be bothered with any further amendments. If it is not then satisfactory, the government will have to take the responsibility of passing the measure as submitted1.

All I am seeking to do now is to pass on to the minister what appears to me to be a conflict in the wording of these two sections. When he gives consideration to what I have said, if he thinks there is nothing in it of course he will not accede to it; on the other hand, if he thinks there is something in it, perhaps he will accept it.
Will the minister not delete the words "who has not abandoned his land" from sub-section 1 of section 68?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that this section is for the purpose of taking care of cases where the soldier has sold his land to a civilian.

I would say at once to the
minister, there is no room for doubt in that case at all.

In such a case surely the
soldier's agreement must first have been determined.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that the section is to cover the case of a settler who has sold his land

abandoning it *-under a three party agreement. Clearly, we do not intend to deal with any but soldiers.

The phrase "abandoning his
land" will not cover that case at all.

Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
*friend would not suggest that either the settler -or the man who succeeded him should be given consideration?

No, I only suggest that the
phrase does not cover the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I move that the committee rise and report progress. May I say that I am very thankful for the kind expressions of opinion respecting this bill, but I want to add, Sir, that when this measure comes down again the government will accept full responsibility for it, and I trust the committee will be ready to pass it without very much further discussion. I am going to amend the bill to meet what I think is the consensus of opinion of hon. members, but I certainly do not expect to spend another two or three hours over it.

May I ask whether the
minister has given consideration to the point I raised with regard to the particular situation -of those soldier settlers who have gone on orchard lands? I have been waiting for him to reach clause (c) so that I might again raise the point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has moved that the committee rise, therefore any discussion is out of order.

May I not speak to the
motion, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I propose to look carefully into the suggestion.
The minister proposes to take it into consideration in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House
spent nearly a day on the second reading of the Old Age Pensions resolution. Possibly lion, members would be agreeable to allow the second reading to pass in order to get the resolution into committee. We would like to make a little progress to-day.
I think my right hon. friend should allow that to stand. It is a very important matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is only the
second reading of the resolution. It has still to be discussed in committee, and the bill founded on it has still to be introduced.

I quite appreciate that,
still we must have some notice in view of the importance of this measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All right.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Duff in the chair.
Department of Labour-Annuities Act, $5,000.

Mr. Chairman, it is certainly
a relief to find a reduction. Perhaps the minister will tell us how he is able to properly carry out the necessary work in connection with this item and at the same time cut off S15.000.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this expenditure covers disbursements for travelling and advertising. The reduction is madte because it is not expected that there will be any extensive expenditure for advertising this year.

The Annuities Act has
never been given its proper place in the life of the country, and I am surprised that my hon. friend, coming in with all the zeal of a a new minister, is desirous of cutting down the operations of his department with respect to this act. I cannot very well understand why the act should be under the Labour department. The Annuities Act of Canada is a fine thing, and should be promoted by the government, but I think it should be under a department which has offices in every part of the Dominion; in my humble judgment it should be under the Post Office Department, which I think is the plan adopted in the Old Country. We should have some statement of policy by the government as to whether they intend to go on with this scheme and push it. People who buy annuities under such a scheme as this are relieved of all anxiety for their old age; they get back everything without any expense, and it seems to me that instead of embarking upon a very expensive scheme of old age pensions this act should be helped in order to make it really worth while. I do not say one should be assisted to the exclusion of the other, but I do say that this act has never been given its fair share of public esteem. Will the government say whether or not the Annuities Act is to be shelved, to make room for the much more pretentious scheme of old age pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
There is no intention on
the part of the government to shelve the Annuities Act. I quite agree that it is an excellent act and an important one, but we are
Supply-Labour

able to reduce the expenditure as it has been reduced in the estimates-which I may tell the committee very frankly were very largely prepared before I assumed control of the department-because it was thought that without any impairment of the usefulness of the act we could dispense with the sum which has hitherto been expended in advertising.

I notice that the Post Office Department is now embarking on a large scheme of advertising; that is a department with a monopoly in its own field, and in my judgment it does not require any advertising at all. The Annuities Act should be made popular, and the only way in which that can be done is by publicity, bringing the advantages of the act before the public. I would suggest that the minister give some consideration to this matter before his next estimates come up-if they ever do come up-in order to see whether this act cannot be brought before the public as it should be.
I	would like to ask the minister how many new annuities were purchased during the past year. Perhaps we might have the list for the past five years in order to show in some degree whether the act is popular with the public or whether they are leaving it alone, as I am afraid they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The total annuities purchased for the year 1925-1926 numbered 669, with a total value of $1,945,571, as compared with 486 annuities in 1924-1925 with a value of $1,606,665.
Would the minister please tell the committee how the appropriation was expended last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It was expended as follows: travelling expenses, $315.05; advertising, $60; printing and stationery, $916.44; telegrams, 80 cents; commissions paid to postmasters, $1,534.85; sundries, $56.14, and outstanding advances, $1.55, a total of $2,884.83 to March 17, 1926.

I understand that it is the
policy of the department, so far as possible, to sell these annuities at cost. I remember well a discussion which took place some two years ago; I cannot recall the
II	p.m. figures, but it seems to me that a
very decided profit was shown in the sale of annuities, and the then minister intimated in the House that he had under consideration a possible revision of the basis upon which the cost of the annuities was worked out. I do not know whether the minister has had time to consider that question, or whether he is familiar with it. Can

he inform the committee as to the financial state of the balance sheet for the past year in this connection? If the department is making a considerable profit, would it not be advisable to reduce the cost of the annuities? I remember inquiring into that cost, and I found it fairly high. The minister informed the House that possibly the time had arrived when some reduction in the cost of those annuities could be worked out. I think the cost is figured on a certain rate of interest, and the idea was that that rate might be varied, which would result in a lower cost to the purchasers. I am sure we all agree that this is a most excellent way for people to invest their money and to be assured of an income for the rest of their days. It should be made as convenient as possible, and I think the policy of the government should be to operate that branch as nearly at cost as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I may say that that is
the policy.
Can the minister give us some idea of the condition of the balance sheet for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I shall be glad to furnish
my hon. friend with that information; I do not have it at hand.

I asked the minister for details of the expenditure of last year, when $20,000 was voted. The items which he gave the committee amount to only about $3,000, and I wanted the particulars of the whole expenditure making up the $20,000 voted last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I have already given the
items of expenditure.
Out of the $20.000?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Yes. The advertising was
not proceeded with; it was not considered necessary last year, and that amount was not expended.
Then what was the total expenditure last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
What I have already
stated, $2,884.83.

And this year
it is $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: We are asking for $5,000.

Then you are
asking for more this year, and there is not a

Supply-Labour
241:
decrease of 815,000. What did the minister mean when he said that there was a decrease of 815,000?
'Mr. ELLIOTT:	If my hon. friend will
notice, the estimate for last year was 820,000, which amount was voted. We are asking for a vote of $5,000 this year, a decrease of $15,000.

But there is an
increase in the expenditure, perhaps?

If I remember this act
correctly it was introduced by the late Sir Richard Cartwright. I would like to ask the minister if there has been any revision of the rates since that time. Conditions have changed considerably during the last twenty years.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: There has been no revision, so far as I am aware.	,
Is any revision contemplated by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Not that I know of.

That is exactly what I wanted to follow up. I remember the then minister two or three years ago promising that consideration would be given to this matter, and I should like to find out if the department has done that. If not why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My information is that
the matter has been discussed. It was suggested that there should be some revision, but it is found that the rates are as nearly correct as possible. Consequently there has been no revision so far as I am aware.

If that decision has been
reached it must be because little or no profit was being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The rates were as near
cost as possible.

If the business has been increasing as the minister points out there must have been some increase of profit. This feature is very important in the interest of the people who want to purchase annuities. I do not care whether the discussion comes under this item or some other item, but we ought to know just what money has been made by the department in this connection in the last year, in fact for three or four years, because the surplus must be piling up.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I shall be very glad to get that information for my hon. friend.
Would the minister inform the committee when the administration of the Annuities Act came under the Department of Labour, and what department it was under prior to that, time?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I understand that formerly it was under the Department of Trade and Commerce and later the Post Office Department. It was brought under the Department of Labour in 1922.

May I ask the minister whether in the matter of sales the annuities have not been a failure, and if that is not largely due to the fact that people can get more advantageous terms from insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: There has been a substantial increase in the number of contracts. I could give my hon. friend a list of the contracts for the various dates starting with 1909. Since that year the contracts have been increasing steadily.
Would the minister please give them?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

speechtext: Going back to 1924-25, and following up what the minister has said, it would seem that there is a deliberate purpose on the part of the government to let this Annuities Act die. In the report of the Auditor General tabled this session we find that in 1924-25 the sum of $19,922.94 was spent in advertising the act. Last year nothing was spent, and according to the estimate now before us it is not intended that anything shall be spent during the current year. In other words no further effort is to be made to push the scheme. I support what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Boys), that the annuities scheme should be well advertised in the post offices in every town, village and hamlet. I am confident that if this was done there would be a very large increase in the number of those who are taking advantage of this splendid opportunity to provide for their own future.

I have no desire to hold this item up, but I ask the minister under what item we may get the information we have sought and when further discussion can take place with respect to this feature so important from the two angles to which I have referred. If we can be sure of getting the desired information, and if the minister will agree to discuss the matter in connection with some other item, I have no desire to hold the vote up at the moment. But the minister must give us some idea as to how this will be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I give my hon. friend the assurance that in connection with the Conciliation and Labour Act vote the information asked for will be brought down.

And this discussion will be
continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes.

Some years ago I got
some information in regard to these annuities and found out that a man could obtain a great income if he invested his money in government bonds. Furthermore, he would have something to bequeath on his death. There must be something wrong in connection with the government annuities scheme, because the annuities are not selling as they should. I should like the minister to look into that.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The great increase in the number of annuities being sold indicates that my hon. friend's statement is scarcely correct.

The increase is so small compared with the population served by

the act that I do not think the minister and the department can claim very much credit. We have had very little explanation from the minister, but I quite appreciate the fact that as yet probably he does not know very much about the matter. The department is more or less dormant

I think that is a fail conclusion to arrive at-and it is dormant by reason of a lack of publicity. I do not think you can sell insurance or anything else unless you have publicity and go after the business. It is quite apparent that no energy has been displayed by the government in going after the business, and there has been insufficient publicity. I have never sold insurance but often I think I could. There are two requisites necessary to success-publicity, and an aggressive selling campaign. Apparently in this case we have not had either of these requisites. I consider this a fine-scheme and I am rather anxious about it. Will the minister consider an active selling policy and an active publicity campaign? L would be willing to vote him the $20,000 if he would use it for the right purpose. L would like to have some assurance from, the minister that he will look into the question of the cost of the annuity and the cost to the country as well. If the interest is too high he will have his actuary-and I presume there is an actuary in charge of this scheme-go over the figures, and if it is found, as I think it will be, that the scheme-could be placed before the public in a proper way, he should so place it for -the benefit of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The increase over last
year has been from 486 contracts, amounting to $1,606,665.03, to 669 contracts, amounting to $1,945,571.12. I do not think he will suggest that that is not a good increase. But I shall be very glad indeed to consider the suggestion my hon. friend has made, probably in the supplementary estimates.

What is the total cash on
hand to meet the various contracts?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will use
up the value of the item in the time we are discussing it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
